# Euromonitor: who is winning in the healthspan economy: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Nick Stene - Euromonitor - Healthspan Summit", https://otter.ai/u/I6bgV_HNiWcf94HGErPRO0tu7Hs, recorded 10 Nov 2026 09:24, 23m 32s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Stephen Daniells (NutraIngredients): Okay, so our first speaker is going to set the scene for us. Nick Steen is senior global insight manager for consumer health for Euro Monitor, and he's going to tell us who is winning in the health fan economy. Thank you. Thank you.
[00:20] Speaker 1 (Nick Stene): Good morning. Right. So my name's Nick. I'll get into who I am in a minute. I've got 20 minutes, and in that time, I wish to impart three things. One, where is the money going? Second thing, who's getting paid, and what messages are actually winning premium. So I'll show you some growth numbers, and I'll show you which prices are actually achieved in the market around particular claims and ingredients. And lastly, I want to just emphasize the proof topic. It is probably the most important thing strategically going on within the BBS space right now, and I'll get around to explaining why. If I look at background, so I've got 30 years doing business decision making, 20 brand side, then 10 in research consulting, and I'm a psychologist. I mention that just because you'll notice it creeps in every now and again into how I think and how I talk about these things. First of all, some context. So if we look at the total industry, we've got as I scope it, we've got a total value of 373 billion vitamins and dietary supplements as one of the big growth areas. If we look at it within the pie chart for size, you can see how it breaks out. OTC treatments, sports nutrition, and weight management and well-being. It's currently about 5% growth. If you take out inflation, it's 1.5. That's down half a point into further stagnation overall if we rip out prices. So this is this is not a fast demand growth environment where some parts of it are actually growing faster than others. If we look particularly at that treatment area, rip out inflation, and that's actually gone negative this year, and that's created one of the first big things I want to just mention, which is this is the first year in which we have spent more physically on prevention than we have on treatment. That's quite a big milestone in terms of changes to the market. And if you look at the difference between VDS and OTC, that gap is only going to get bigger. Then let's look at that in future terms. So this is looking at the cash added between now and 2031 from all the forecast data that we pick up from our partners. And if we look at the immediate growth year on year, that's 2027 versus this year. If we look long term, this is an average K gap out to 2031, and the bubble size is the cash. It's the size of the prize that will be added between now and 2031. And one of the things that jumps out is yes, there's some bubbles which are more attractive than others, but then let's add a cost element to this. So OTC has been hit by the tariffs more than the rest of the health industry. If we then think about what's going on in the Middle East, the dependence on the active pharmaceutical ingredients coming out of India, coming out of China, are creating a greater liability. So the cost of that, the disruption of that has been greater for treatment than it has for VDS, and the future one is around the European wastewater. Again, that's intended to hit the OTC space more than it is going to hit the prevention space in VDS. So that that's a nice big block of value for OTC, but it's got quite serious profit questions around it in terms of the business model and going forward. Then let's look at the protein one around sports protein products. This is then getting hit by the problems with premium weight, and I've got data showing the shelf a 20% plus pass through in physical pricing, but that's 30 to 40% overall. If you then take into account shrinkage in packaging and all the other techniques that the brands are trying to do to actually absorb this cost. So the protein one probably starts to get solved in supply because it's scarcity driven around premium way around 2027 back end, 2028 earliest, and that's starting to get solved. There's years of trauma left inside of that one, so that block also has questions in terms of future profit. So that makes the block for dietary supplements even more attractive. This is revenue, but if we think in profit terms, that's actually the most attractive by a long way for a lot of what's going on, and that is then leading to a migration of money heading towards dietary supplements, particularly premium dietary supplements. Both we can see it within line extensions, we can see it inside with brand actions at the tactical level, but at the strategic level, we also see it driving mergers and acquisition strategy. And there's quite a lot of finance. I see about eight to $9 billion in motion right now around fighting over positioning. Some of that's coming from outside of health and venture capital and private equity getting involved inside of this to fight over that space. So it's just to let you know that that area is competitive and it's going to become more competitive over time. Then we come to the first speed bump when we're into any topic about health span. What do we actually mean by the term? And I reckon if we got 10 of us up on the stage and asked 10 people what health span is, we would collectively come to 10 different answers. Some will include aspects of it. Some will exclude. It will be an interesting conversation. So, if I think about how I am looking at health span and measuring health span, I'm starting to perceive this as a funnel, and this is coming from the research into how consumers are shopping and how they do message recognition and what they're actually looking for. So, I think at the edge of this funnel, the cutting edge of this area, we've got naming on the product itself. This is the actual SKU name, and it's directly into age. It's directly into life stage. It's directly into the core messaging for what we're here in this room to talk about. And one of the things to point out is mitochondrial is one of the elements that's appearing inside of here. I'll come back to that in a minute. Then we end up with a broader health span messaging that can appear anywhere on the pack. It doesn't necessarily mean that the skew is all about health span. It's touching into the space, and then we've got the protection messages, and this takes us to a much bigger part of the funnel, and this is immune system. It's antioxidant. It's a much broader message structure. We've got to separate them and think of them differently because they've got very different commercial profiles in terms of how well they're doing and who's winning and where that's winning. If I think about that funnel, then across different areas, and I'm going down to 18 markets now because these are the ones with the cleanest data to be able to do the analysis as to what fits and where. So if I look at total value from the supplements, this is from our total market size, and we look at that edge. It's niche, but it's growing. I'll come to growth rates in a second, and yes, you can think it's quite low within Asia, but look at the cash value difference between Asia and Europe, top six. This is where it's playing out in terms of scale. If we then think about the broader health plan messaging, it kicks in at this larger level, and when we get into the protection messaging, we're talking about half the shelf, pretty much. So, in terms of scale, that one aspect of this, but also I did analysis in terms of what's achieving a premium versus the rest of the shelf, and the edge is the part that's actually exceeding the rest of it. The actual broader health span messaging is appearing on cheap product as much as it's appearing on expensive product. There's a degree to which the message is getting diluted as part of the step-up structure at this moment. So the the second thing I really want to get across is we've got to name the need, and the more we name the need, the more we get the benefits out of this space, both on the growth side, but also on the getting paid for it side of it with premium achievement. If we look at growth rates, this is online growth. I'll just state that outright. So the VBS number is probably larger than you're expecting. One of the things to point out is the edge is where we're seeing the exceptional growth, and we do see actual growth within the broader messaging. It's more successful within the shops because of the trust angle than it is online. There's a degree of trust leaking into the online situation around who can you trust, what messages can you trust. People are making incredibly strong promises without a lot of background as to why they make it and the evidence behind it. You could obviously think that it's all about the demographics, but when I tried to correlate and look at all of the things that drive a market that's got a rising health span number within the nutrition side of it, I got some surprises. So it's not really correlating around the existing size of the aging population. That doesn't count, and it's not particularly around the spend on health right now. That didn't really match against where this is growing particularly quickly. I also did a check because when we looked at this in 2022 and 2023, we saw that the COVID scare had led to a large amount of investment heading in this direction that has stopped having any kind of relationship to which markets this is growing in. One of the other things that I did find is actually spend on self-cow and OTC spend that is actually on the border of being statistically significant around a relationship to which markets this is growing in, and there's a logic to that around when we have conditions and we start to spend on condition support. That's the place where effectively the nutritional angle for health plans is going to resonate the most. We've got e-commerce as arising. This is access based, but I didn't see a difference between total shelf VDS and the health plan product. So this is just about access generally, and we get into one of the other aspects where it's it is about the aging population, but it's about how many people enter a new life stage in a given year, and that is actually driving some of this is not to do with the base population right now. It's to do with people arriving at a transitional moment, and I can explain insight. Income was part of it, but it was not that strong apart. I can explain within consumer poll demographics about 30 to 40% of the shift in the growth period. If I look at what else is going on, I think the push side of it and the creation of demand from the brand messaging is explaining about another third or so of the actual growth that we're seeing. And then, when I go into this, I can find anecdotal evidence on the survey side that the relationship between employer and employee is driving another aspect of this. If we think about the price of being ill, it's not just about the symptoms. It's not just about the issues. It's about the time off work, and we are seeing quite a substantial shift in the relationship between employer and employee, and the penalties potentially across the world on being out of work are right, and that is affecting the whole dynamic around why prevention is winning over treatment, and it's actually most manifest within the health span area. So there's an economic aspect to this. It's an investment more than it is actually just something ephemeral and something emotional. There are there are fiscal aspects to this. There are rational aspects to this around protecting income. If we look at what is actually growing, this is growing at the shelf rather than sales growth, just to be clear. So along the x-axis, you see that the rate of new products and messaging arriving at the shelf, and then on the y-axis you can see the premium level that's being achieved. And we can see longevity and healthy aging in the U.S. is the element that's growing fastest and getting paid very strongly followed. I am seeing menopause generally actually losing its premium. It's becoming ubiquitous inside of the messaging, but within it, we do have this new 40 plus element targeting around perimenopause, and that is still achieving a premium. It's not as fast in growth terms. It's not as big a message, but it's coming and it's coming fast. If I then think broader, the menopause and the prostate messaging, prostate aid that men, I'll come to the different life stage messaging in a minute. That started to slow down a little bit, and it's lost the premium. It's back into how many launches are being positioned from value brands and from private label. If we think about the beauty angle to it, so skin is ubiquitous. It's one of the biggest messages inside of this space. It peaked in 2025, and it's actually starting to slow down the new launches and what's coming to market? It's still one of the stronger areas, but behind it, and my my beauty colleagues have warned me, the next big one is hair, and I can see it already within the hair loss treatment space. It's one of the fastest growth categories this year, but I can also see it appearing inside the nutrition element of it, and hair is achieving a premium, and it's actually appearing in weights over the shelf. If we look at the immune system, I'm going to come to magnesium in a second and talk about what's going on with magnesium. But the immune system has also peaked, and it's sitting there. It's just trucking away. It's one of the workhorses of this market in terms of maintaining value and cash scale. If we then go across the pond and we look at Europe, it's roughly the same pattern. One thing jumped out at me, which is slightly different: the messaging around mitochondrial is a lot stronger in Europe already than it is in the U.S. at this stage, and some of this is to do with regulatory framework and what messaging is allowed inside of one process in Nathan. Health span messaging, in and of itself, healthy aging messaging in Europe is a tougher sell, and some of it isn't making it to the physical shelf. Some of it's only occurring online. So different wording, but the same sort of pattern in terms of what's going on. If I think about that magnesium angle, I'm into the issues around ingredients and the lifespan of ingredients commanding a premium. We've got a number of the magnesium variants that are tied to specific need, and what's fascinating in terms of their pattern, they've arrived at the shelf in far greater number, but they've lost their premium in the act of doing so, and they've turned into footballs, and they're being kicked around on price right now, which is, if you look at it, ironic that those are actually achieving less of a premium overall than some of the more basic forms. L3 and eight is escaping this so far. It's attached to the cognitive side of it. It's doing well around launches and into premium achievement. But look at the pattern. If it ends up as another football, it's not going to be long before it actually starts to bleed and lose its premium. So the pattern I can see is we get proof of benefit, we get to premium achievement, we reach popularity, and the scale goes, the awareness rises, and then we're entitled. And this battle has played out a few times within Magnesium so far. And so one of the things is a bit melodramatic as a statement, but popularity is the death knell on premium. It's more complicated than that, but you get the idea. I've also seen it at the cutting edge. So NAD Plus has been the breakout. It escaped niche last year, and we see it growing three times larger on the shelf in the U.S. inside of an 18-month period. So enormous levels of change, and what I see is a recovery-ish in 2026, with greater use of stacks. So NAD plus with spermidine, NAD plus with resveratrol, and a number of other combinations. So we've got back some of the premium as new launches have hit the market. But you can see the general trend with Europe not not far behind in terms of the pattern. I think we're into popularity and we're near to price war. It's still got a premium, but it's lost quite a substantial amount of that premium. And that brings us into one of the structures around trust and proof. If ingredients lose premium over time, what's next? And NAD Plus has been and will continue to be a really strong workhorse in this space. It's got lots of value adds in terms of messaging and what we can do with it in product terms. But what's sitting behind? From what I can see, there's a number of ingredients that might be the next thing. But postbiotics is at this moment in time kicking ass, and if I look at the growth rate, if I look at the messaging it's getting into, it's got really strong connections into GLP-1, and it's achieving one of the strongest premiums at this moment in time. So if I want to point in any one direction, that's the one that's got my attention, and I'm studying that one quite a lot. So what's next? We need a pipeline of premiums. You can't just rely on something to be there and shine forever. If we get into the life stages, so I can see menopause is starting to slow down, but within it, the perimenopause messaging is rising fast. It's on one minute at this point, and that's doubled in a year. Underlying that is the number of ingredients that are driving it. If I look at the male equivalent andropause, blokes do not seem to be buying to a life stretch, so they don't really want the label, and they certainly don't want to walk into a part of the store that's labeled up as Andrew Police Paul. What they do want to talk about is testosterone and performance. I made the mistake of going to one of those sites and dwelling for a couple of minutes, and I'm now being hunted across all of my profiles online with how do I feel like a man and would I like her? How could it's everywhere. I mean, I cannot now go and watch a cat video, which is what the internet was actually designed for. If I look at the the direction, men get a performance message; they also get an organ, and it might not be the one that everyone was expecting. But effectively, the prostate is a sufficient source of fear that it's driving a certain amount of traffic, a certain amount of effort here. I have eight. I talk about them a bit too much. One of the reasons I talk about them so often is because this is one of the most interesting and exciting growth profiles that I have seen in 30 years. So it broke 100 million inside of year one, it's currently on target to hit around 220 to 230 in year two. They are projecting 400 million in year three, and they just picked up. Let's just skip through all the junk. They picked up a billion in investment funding earlier on this year, and it's because of. There we go. They have a subscription model with an acquisition rate that's allowing them to get to a profit level from investment, which is pain all over the market. So that's attracted the investment, and that's why they're going so bullish in terms of their growth. If if you want to study two brands that are absolutely nailing proof, I am eight is one of them. I would also draw your attention to ancient and brave. It is one of the most incredible structures in terms of how how trusted they have made themselves within their loyal shopper base in such a hot tithing. So one of the other things I'm observing is if you are solving a problem, either you'll fix it or you won't. But either one of those leads to you no longer being needed. If instead you're about trying to facilitate someone's perfect life, you're not asking them to admit they're imperfect, which is one of the first things that consumers are struggling with right now. So I think, honestly, what I'm starting to see is this difference in messaging and positioning. It's the same thing. It's collagen, but it's multiple ways of actually communicating collagen, which answer completely different needs in the emotional range. And one of those has got a long-term survival within the human basket. The other one is either going to die because it solved the problem. There's no more problem, or it's failed to fix the problem. So why would I continue taking it? So I've got four takeaways. One, see it with proof. That's the part that's paying. That's the part that's growing. The more specific we get, the more evidence we've got around it, the better. Also, we've got to know the ingredient life stage that we're operating with, and what's the pipeline? What's next? What's coming? We've got to segment and price this. I think we are failing as a species, all women, and we're failing particularly the age band heading into perimenopause. This is from personal experience on the journey with my wife as well. It is an absolute horror show. So I think there's a lot that can be done. Just she didn't get listened to and she didn't get referred to a specialist until I was in the room, and I'm just confused. We we are not doing very well inside of this area. There's a lot more that we can do. It's nice to see that the 40 plus messaging and perimenopause is finally finding voice, but there's a lot more to go inside of this space. summary.Summary:
Nick Stene, Senior Global Insight Manager for consumer health at Euromonitor International, opened the Healthspan Summit. His question was where the money in healthspan is going and which messages earn a premium.

He started with the market. Consumer health grows about 5%, only 1.5% without inflation, and this is the first year more is spent on prevention than on treatment. Medicines sold over the counter and sports protein are both under profit pressure, so money, including billions in deal finance, is moving to premium dietary supplements.

Within healthspan, products that name a specific need or life stage earn a premium, while broad wording appears on cheap and expensive products alike. Ingredients follow a life cycle: proof brings a premium, popularity brings scale, then a price war. Magnesium forms have gone that way and NAD+ is close, with postbiotics leading what queues behind it. IM8, one product meant to replace a shelf of supplements, was his example of a brand winning on proof and trust.

His conclusion: lead with proof, know where each ingredient is in its life cycle, segment and price for specific groups such as women entering perimenopause, and design proof for shoppers, healthcare professionals and the AI agents that will increasingly shop for them.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Milestone: "the first year in which we have spent more physically on prevention than we have on treatment", and the gap between supplements and OTC will widen [00:20] (photo 2).
- Money is moving to premium dietary supplements, through line extensions, brand actions and M&A; he sees "about eight to $9 billion in motion", some from venture capital and private equity outside health [00:20].
- Healthspan as a funnel: the edge (SKU names directly on age and life stage, including mitochondrial) is niche, growing and earns a premium; broader healthspan wording appears on cheap and expensive products alike; protection messages (immune, antioxidant) cover about half the shelf [00:20].
- Ingredient life cycle: proof of benefit, then premium, then popularity, then price war. Magnesium forms "turned into footballs" on price, while L-threonate, the cognitive form, still holds a premium; "popularity is the death knell on premium" [00:20] (photo 3).
- NAD+ is losing its premium as it goes mainstream (US price index 1.84 in 2024, 1.43 in 2026 to date); postbiotics lead what queues behind it, with share up 48% and a price index of 2.83 [00:20] (photo 4).
- IM8 is the fastest year-one growth he has seen: one product of 90 ingredients positioned to replace 16 supplements, with year-two revenue guidance of USD 220 to 230 million [00:20] (photo 7).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- His whey supply timing is recorded in Detail as he said it, but our whey market view rests on Alan Johnstone's account at SANS Europe (unfiltered-an-insider-s-view-of), not on this talk (Nathan, 10 Nov 2026).
- His ingredient life cycle applies to creatine: proof brings a premium and popularity erodes it [00:20] (photo 3). My reading: CreaWin's case to brands should rest on its own evidence and a clear benefit, not on creatine's popularity.
- Healthy-ageing customers pay for named needs and proof, and in Europe mitochondrial wording is already established [00:20]. My reading: our healthy-ageing pitches should name the need and the evidence.
- AI shopping agents read proof differently [00:20]. My reading: our evidence files should be structured and machine-readable.
- Relevance high: healthy-ageing market structure and sports protein economics.

files.name: otter-summary.md
files.text:
Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

Nick presents an analysis of the healthspan economy, highlighting a strategic shift from disease treatment to preventive dietary supplements.

## Market Dynamics
**Nick** outlines a significant transition in the consumer health industry, noting that for the first time, spending on prevention has surpassed spending on treatment. While the total vitamins and dietary supplements (VDS) market is valued at $373 billion, growth is uneven. 
*   **OTC** treatments face challenges including tariffs, supply chain dependencies on India and China, and environmental regulations regarding wastewater.
*   **Sports nutrition** faces profit pressures due to high protein costs and packaging shrinkage.
*   **Dietary supplements** are identified as the most attractive segment for investment and mergers/acquisitions, with $8 to $9 billion currently in motion via venture capital and private equity.

## Growth Drivers
**Nick** identifies several key areas driving premium pricing and market expansion:
*   **Healthspan Messaging:** Consumers are moving toward specific "edge" messaging such as mitochondrial health, rather than broad protection messages like immunity. 
*   **Life Stages:** There is rapid growth in perimenopause targeting (40+ demographic), whereas general menopause messaging is losing its premium. For men, the focus shifts from "andropause" labels to testosterone and performance.
*   **Ingredient Trends:** **NAD Plus** has seen massive growth in the U.S., though it is entering a phase where price wars may occur. **Postbiotics** are currently performing strongly with high premiums due to connections with **GLP-1**.
*   **Beauty & Hair:** While skin messaging is peaking, hair loss treatment is emerging as a fast-growing category that commands a premium.

## Strategic Takeaways
To maintain profitability, **Nick** suggests brands must move beyond simple problem-solving to facilitating a "perfect life" through emotional positioning. He emphasizes three critical pillars for success:
*   **Proof:** Brands must provide specific evidence and clinical backing to justify premium prices.
*   **Segmentation:** Companies must identify which life stage or specific ingredient cycle they are entering to avoid the "popularity death knell" where mass adoption erodes margins.
*   **Gatekeepers:** Success requires winning over three distinct groups: the shopper, healthcare professionals, and the emerging "agentic commerce" AI agents.

How can brands effectively design proof that satisfies both human healthcare professionals and automated AI shopping agents?

Action items (Otter's): none.

Growth by category, 2025 then 2026: vitamins and dietary supplements 5.9% and 5.6%; OTC 3.4% and 3.2%; sports nutrition 13.3% and 12.5%; weight management and wellbeing 0.2% and 0.3%. OTC is hit hardest by tariffs, by dependence on active pharmaceutical ingredients from India and China, and, next, by European wastewater rules [00:20].

Sports protein, as he said it: he has shelf data showing a 20% plus pass-through in physical pricing, 30 to 40% overall once pack shrinkage and other absorption moves are counted. On premium whey supply: "So the protein one probably starts to get solved in supply because it's scarcity driven around premium way around 2027 back end, 2028 earliest", with "years of trauma" left [00:20].

Growth is stronger in shops than online, where trust is leaking; demographics explain about 30 to 40% of growth (people entering a new life stage, not the size of the ageing population), brand push about another third, and employers' attitudes to time off work more [00:20].

On the US shelf, longevity and healthy ageing grow fastest and earn a strong premium; menopause is losing its premium while 40-plus and perimenopause still earn one; prostate has lost its premium; skin peaked in 2025 and hair is next; immune has peaked but remains a workhorse [00:20].

Europe follows the same pattern, but mitochondrial messaging is already stronger than in the US, partly because of what the regulatory framework allows, and healthy-ageing messaging is "a tougher sell", some of it only online [00:20].

Postbiotics are growing fast, have "really strong connections into GLP-1" and earn one of the strongest premiums; he is watching them most closely. In his words: "But postbiotics is at this moment in time kicking ass" [00:20].

Life stage, US products per 10,000 supplement products, 2024, 2025 and 2026 to date: testosterone 171, 182, 163; prostate 70, 85, 98; menopause 46, 64, 73; andropause 0, 1, 2. He named IM8 and Ancient + Brave as brands nailing proof [00:20]. Nathan's note: IM8 "is winning a lot in the market, alongside Ancient+Brave" (notes).

Positioning that facilitates "someone's perfect life" lasts longer than solving a problem, which ends when it is fixed or fails; collagen can be sold either way [00:20]. The slide sets "something wrong [with] you our product can fix" (joints, wrinkles, ageing, collagen deficiency) against "Aspire to a life free of imperfection" (vitality, performance, radiance, wellbeing): "you never stop taking something that is part of who you want to be" (photo 8).

His takeaways: lead with proof; know the ingredient's life stage and the pipeline behind it; segment and price, with women heading into perimenopause badly served; and design proof for three gatekeepers: shoppers, healthcare professionals and agentic commerce [00:20].

takeaways.text: Milestone: "the first year in which we have spent more physically on prevention than we have on treatment", and the gap between supplements and OTC will widen [00:20] (photo 2).

Money is moving to premium dietary supplements, through line extensions, brand actions and M&A; he sees "about eight to $9 billion in motion", some from venture capital and private equity outside health [00:20].

Healthspan as a funnel: the edge (SKU names directly on age and life stage, including mitochondrial) is niche, growing and earns a premium; broader healthspan wording appears on cheap and expensive products alike; protection messages (immune, antioxidant) cover about half the shelf [00:20].

Ingredient life cycle: proof of benefit, then premium, then popularity, then price war. Magnesium forms "turned into footballs" on price, while L-threonate, the cognitive form, still holds a premium; "popularity is the death knell on premium" [00:20] (photo 3).

NAD+ is losing its premium as it goes mainstream (US price index 1.84 in 2024, 1.43 in 2026 to date); postbiotics lead what queues behind it, with share up 48% and a price index of 2.83 [00:20] (photo 4).
IM8 is the fastest year-one growth he has seen: one product of 90 ingredients positioned to replace 16 supplements, with year-two revenue guidance of USD 220 to 230 million [00:20] (photo 7).

# A Bigger Sports Nutrition Landscape: Growth, Tensions and What Comes Next: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Nick Morgan - Sports Nutrition Sunmit", https://otter.ai/u/Pxd86SRFpBSZ2lO7RwpmypP_fpQ, recorded 9 Nov 2026 09:09, 27m 6s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Speaker 1: To William, read nutrient greetings for the invitation to speak. Hopefully, this will be interesting for you today in terms of thinking about sport, nutrition, and a state of the nation. I explicitly looked to bring through a couple of words in the title just to talk about a bigger landscape because I know that is something that you're all thinking about. Of course, we intrinsically always talk about sport interactive, and by definition, that means a lot of people, more people than ever that you could potentially engage with, whether brands, ingredient suppliers, content manufacturers, or flavor houses, or anybody in between. I also just want to point you to the direction of the word tensions. I think that is also very important. I could stand up here today and deliver an incredible story of something that's going to be huge, and everyone in this world could win in. But of course, with growth comes tensions, and everyone needs to think clearly about what this future looks like. Now, as I get through this, I just want to say that ultimately, my aim today is to help you make sense of the trends, honestly, I don't think it takes a genius to stand up here and say that protein is important, or longevity is front of mind, or hydration has become something for everybody, or that GLP-1 is something we're going to talk about for most of the afternoon. To be honest, I've got eight boxes on here, and they all refer to something that could be really interesting for you today. I could have put another eight boxes and genuinely could have made a story about each and every one of them. So if you're in magnesium and you're not on there, I apologize. You could be on there. If you're in gut health and probiotics, you're not on there, but you could be, and there's an opportunity. These are just eight of some things we talk about, but I just want to refer back to the statement of sports nutrition is going mainstream, and just say, well, obviously it is. But I just want to put three questions on there, and just try to make sure everyone thinks through this carefully. That is, but is sports nutrition growing beyond the motivations that defined it? I think it is, and that's an important thing to reflect on. Is sports nutrition winning the consumer? I think it is, but is it losing its identity? That's not a negative, by the way. I'm just probing some things that you need to think about. And is the market growing, or are we just moving the boundaries? And that's actually a really important point to think through as well, because in some respects we will continue to think through the terms of sports nutrition going mainstream. It's becoming more active, therefore you can sell protein to anyone, and I genuinely believe you possibly could. But these statements just really are quite pointed to think and to push you to think about what that means. Now I will say from the outset that a lot of this feels like I'm going to be talking to brands, but I'm actually going to be talking to everyone in the room through the lens of ingredient suppliers and cotton manufacturers too, and I'll try to make that relevant throughout. Now, when I put those three questions up there, this is one of the most talked-about things that I think I must have spoken about over the last 12 months. So, apologies for those that have seen me present before, or work with us closely as a company, but Starbucks creating a cold foam delivering 15 grams of protein to add on top of your americano is one of the most talked-about trends of 2026. It started in Q4 2025, started in America, moved into the UK. It's in Central Europe. You can get it in Singapore. You can get it in India. Albeit protein source changes. A really important point here is that a bigger market does not simply mean more of the same market. That's a really important point when thinking through the trends. This is a sports nutrition ingredient by definition. It's protein. It's an everyday coffee ritual, though. It's a different competitive arena. summary.Summary:
Nick Morgan of Nutrition Integrated opened the day with a state of the market. Sports nutrition is obviously going mainstream, he said, but is it growing beyond the motivations that defined it, is it winning consumers while losing its identity, and is the market growing or are its boundaries just moving?

He answered with three rules. Growth does not guarantee value: whey protein prices have never been higher, and brands are going through a structural reset, cutting promotions, shrinking packs, reformulating, launching whey hybrids and trying to sell more higher-margin lines such as creatine and electrolytes. Relevance does not guarantee ownership: creatine is now for everyone, in gummies, chocolate and products for women, and hydration has no agreed formula and new leaders. Opportunity does not guarantee advantage: his company tracks 16,412 product listings in eight categories, and only a few products will succeed, by pulling on format, brand, dose, science and branded ingredients.

His conclusion was that the principles of sports nutrition have gone mainstream, not sports nutrition itself. Brands should think beyond the category, stay true to the industry's DNA, choose where to compete and know their right to win. Everyone has a seat at the table, but not everyone will win.

"Other" (liquids, foods, chocolate) grew fastest off a tiny base, and most brands now have a route into broader retail [25:59]. Examples: Creatonics' "Creatine+ formulated for women" sachet and Sunday Natural's Nutrachoc creatine chocolate, 20 pieces at 1,000 mg creatine monohydrate, sweetened with tagatose (photo 14) (photo 15).
- Hydration: no agreed electrolyte dose (SiS "all five essential", LMNT 1,000 mg sodium, Precision by sweat rate); Liquid IV is the category leader at £1.50 a stick; effervescents are three times cheaper than a stick pack [00:00]. Shelf prices: Liquid I.V. GBP 1.50 a sachet (GBP 9.00 for 6; GBP 1.00 on Clubcard), Phizz GBP 0.40 a tablet (GBP 8.00 for 20; GBP 0.28 on Clubcard), Evian 750 ml GBP 1.85, Red Bull 250 ml GBP 2.10, Lucozade Sport 500 ml GBP 1.65, each single (photo 16).
- Declared sodium a serve on selected electrolyte powders: 38 mg (ViDrate Boost), 350 mg (SiS Hydro+), 500 mg (Cadence Daily), 570 mg (Liquid I.V. Multiplier), 750 mg (Hunter & Gather), 1,000 mg (LMNT). 69% of powders include four or five electrolytes; 8% claim Himalayan sea salt as a natural sodium source. The slide: "there is no optimal formula" [00:00] (photo 18).
- Hydration powders are positioned three ways: everyday (Humantra, Hunter & Gather, Repowr: routine, natural, sugar-free), superior (SOS "4x faster than water", Ancient + Brave, ARTAH "cellular hydration") and performance (226ERS Hydra Zero on sweat losses, HIGH5 Isotonic carbs plus electrolytes, Precision PH strength options) (photo 22).
- Naturalness: 40% state natural colours, 46% use natural flavours, 43% include stevia. Humantra names grape skin as its colour source, Liquid I.V. declares sugar alongside steviol glycosides, ViDrate covers flavour, colour and sweetening in one proposition, Cadence extends the absence message to fillers [00:00] (photo 24).
- Tracked listings (US and Europe, 16,412 across eight spaces): creatine 3,448 (new-product activity +10% over the latest six months), magnesium 2,833 (+15%), collagen 2,648, energy and focus 2,153, pre-workout 1,869, sleep and mood 1,626, electrolyte 1,487, longevity 348 (+20% new). From the stage: almost 3,500 creatine, almost 2,800 magnesium, over 2,500 collagen. "Only a few will be really successful" [00:00] (photo 23).
- Branded ingredient penetration (share of tracked products with at least one identified branded ingredient): pre-workout 53% (many use more than one), longevity 40%, energy and focus 31%, sleep and mood 25%, creatine 25%, collagen 25%, electrolyte 17%, magnesium 17%. The slide adds that minerals in general are "needing to work harder to prove the benefit" [18:50] (photo 27).
- Longevity takes three approaches: alter the ageing process (cellular health, mitochondria, senescence), optimise the ageing experience (muscle and mobility, cognition, energy, sleep) or personalise to a life stage (ageing athletes, menopause, later life). Example: Cellaro's Vitalize AM, Renew PM and Reset monthly range against the 12 hallmarks of ageing [18:50] (photo 29).
- Longevity and athlete-backed brands compete for the same consumer: Sergio Ramos links sport to longevity through Centenarian ("Real longevity, backed by science. To perform better. To live better."), with normal sports products framed as living better today. The competitive set has never been broader [18:50] (photo 30).
- Brands should engage with gut and microbiome, longevity and GLP-1, but stay true to the industry's DNA; this will be "the biggest challenge you face for your budgets and strategy in 2027 and beyond" [18:50].
- The four closing principles: think beyond the category (new consumers, needs and occasions); stay true to your DNA (capabilities, credibility, differentiation); choose where to compete ("where you could play from where you should play"); know your right to win (where you can create distinctive value). "Growth creates opportunity. Understanding change creates advantage." [18:50] (photo 32)

Whey protein price mitigation
From cyclical volatility to structural reset. The industry response is rapidly evolving beyond tactical pricing mitigation. While immediate actions buy time, long-term resilience and profitability increasingly depend on reformulation, alternative protein architectures (such as plant and hybrid blends), and diversification into non-whey adjacent functional nutrition.
01 / TACTICAL Price Increases. Benefits: Some margin recovery; Simple to implement. Limitations: Price elasticity risks; Retailer pushback; Competitive disadvantage. Observation: Widespread across market.
02 / TACTICAL Reduce Promo. Benefits: Protects base margins; Limits low-margin volume. Limitations: Lower sales velocities; Reduced shelf visibility; Consumer friction. Observation: Increasingly common.
03 / TACTICAL Pack Architecture. Benefits: Lowers absolute price; Retains entry-level buyers. Limitations: Smaller/fewer servings; Unit price inflation risk; Overall volume risk. Observation: Widely adopted globally.
04 / STRATEGIC Reformulation. Benefits: Structural cost reduction; Margin resilience. Limitations: Sensory/taste profile risks; Potential trust issues; Adjacent price volatility. Observation: Brand specific activity.
05 / FUTURE FOCUS New Products. Benefits: Decreases whey reliance; Unlock plant & hybrid. Limitations: Ground zero revenue base; Consumer education; Taste expectations. Observation: Top priority for brands.
06 / FUTURE FOCUS Portfolio Shift. Benefits: Sell other products; Creatine, Energy, Fibre. Limitations: Brand permission; Alienate core consumers; May not replace revenue. Observation: Top priority for brands.
Figure 5. The strategic choices brands are working through in order to mitigate the impact of high whey protein prices. 02. Growth > Value

Rocka range. Pro Protein: "Vegan Performance Protein". Higher protein dose (24g) + a slightly higher calorie content (122kcals) to achieve a "smooth, creamy, indulgent taste". 83% plant protein blend [fava bean & pea]. EUR 37.99 per 700g tub [EUR 1.65 per serve].

A difference in electrolyte opinion
HOW BRANDS EXPLAIN THEIR ELECTROLYTES (Approach: Explanation and brand example)
Number & completeness: SiS highlights five essential electrolytes. Number reassures, and the premise of "comprehensive" seems intuitive.
Sweat-loss replacement: Veloforte links minerals to sweat losses, giving electrolytes a clear purpose and reason to choose.
Dose & strength: LMNT promotes a meaningful dose. Explain who it suits, rather than implying that more means better.
Blend, ratio & science: Bulk promotes optimum ratios, communicating why the chosen blend is right for the need.
Personal relevance: Precision matches strengths to sweat losses, helping consumers choose the right product for their needs.
Natural sources & wider benefits: Hunter & Gather uses natural minerals and daily balance, adding reasons to buy beyond the blend.
SIMILAR BREADTH, DIFFERENT DOSES. 69% of powders include four or five electrolytes (footnote 1).
Sodium per serve varies widely. Selected powders, declared sodium (mg/serve): ViDrate Boost 38 mg; SiS Hydro+ 350 mg; Cadence Daily 500 mg; Liquid I.V. Multiplier 570 mg; Hunter & Gather 750 mg; LMNT 1000 mg. Axis 0 to 1200.
Selected products, not the full-category distribution. *8% of products claim Himalayan sea salt as a natural approach to sodium.

To alter, optimise or personalise
01 ALTER: The ageing process. Target the biological hallmarks of ageing. Cellular health, mitochondria, senescence.
02 OPTIMISE: The ageing experience. Preserve physical, cognitive and emotional capability. Muscle & mobility, cognition, energy, sleep.
03 PERSONALISE: The age focus. Tailor longevity to consumer needs and life stage. Ageing athletes, menopause, later life.
Example: Cellaro range (Vitalize AM, Renew PM, Reset monthly) against the 12 Hallmarks of Aging. VITALIZE, your daily cellular fuel: consistent daytime energy; clear, steady focus; better post-workout recovery; built for long-term vitality. RESET, your monthly cellular clean-up: senescent-cell clean-up; calms inflammaging signals; aids day-to-day recovery; supports long-term cellular renewal. RENEW, your nightly cellular repair: nightly cellular clean up (autophagy); calms inflammation signals; PM anti-oxidant defense; long term cellular rejuvenation.

Making sense of the trends (closing version)
The principles of sports nutrition are going mainstream. Period
WHEY: Price pressure | CREATINE: Booming interest | PROTEIN: Everywhere | HYDRATION: Beyond exercise
GLP-1: New nutrition needs | LONGEVITY: Healthspan focus | WOMEN: Wider relevance | FITNESS: More ways to be active
...but sports nutrition is growing beyond the motivations that defined it

files.text:
Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

Nick Morgan discusses the evolution of sports nutrition as it moves into the mainstream and explores the resulting market tensions.

## Market Evolution
**Nick** argues that sports nutrition is expanding beyond its original motivations, moving from niche athletic use to everyday consumption. He highlights several key shifts:
*   **Mainstream Integration**: The **Starbucks** protein-infused coffee trend serves as a primary example of sports ingredients entering daily rituals.
*   **Identity Shifts**: As the category grows, there is a risk of losing its core identity while simultaneously winning a broader consumer base.
*   **Expanding Boundaries**: The market is not just growing in volume but is redefining its boundaries through new categories like longevity and gut health.

## Industry Tensions
**Nick** outlines significant challenges regarding value, relevance, and competition within the current landscape.
**Protein Dynamics**
The high cost of whey protein has triggered a structural reset among brands. To manage margins, companies are utilizing several strategies:
*   **Whey Hybrids**: Products that blend whey with cheaper sources like milk, soy, or yeast while still marketing as whey-based.
*   **New Formats**: The rise of "whey milkshakes" and collagen-blended proteins to extend product benefits.
*   **Alternative Sources**: Emerging interest in yeast, mycelium, and even protein made from air.
*   **Cost Management**: Brands are using pack architecture changes (e.g., 900g instead of 1kg) and reformulation to offset costs.

**Competitive Landscape**
The sheer volume of products—including 3,500 creatine products and 2,800 magnesium products—creates massive confusion. **Nick** notes that while opportunity is high, advantage is not guaranteed due to extreme competition.
*   **Hydration**: The market is fragmented between different electrolyte approaches (sodium-focused vs. sweat-rate focused) and formats like stick packs versus cheaper effervescent tablets.
*   **Longevity**: There is a growing intersection between sports performance and aging, exemplified by athletes like **Sergio Ramos** linking sports nutrition to cellular health.

## Strategic Outlook
The presentation concludes by emphasizing that brands must navigate "permission to play" in new territories without losing their DNA.
*   **Differentiation**: Success requires leveraging branded ingredients, science-backed narratives, and unique delivery formats such as gummies or functional foods.
*   **Future Focus**: Companies must prepare for how trends like **GLP-1** and the microbiome will influence consumer behavior through 2027.

His four closing principles for winning in a bigger market.

detail.text: His three opening questions: is sports nutrition growing beyond the motivations that defined it, winning consumers but losing its identity, and is the market growing or are the boundaries moving [00:00] (photo 31). His three rules: growth does not guarantee value, relevance does not guarantee ownership, opportunity does not guarantee advantage [00:00].
Starbucks' protein cold foam (15 g) started in Q4 2025 in America and is now in the UK, Central Europe, Singapore and India [00:00].

Raw whey prices on Vesper's EU index: WPI from about EUR 11/kg in January 2023 to EUR 30.5 by July 2026, WPC80 from about EUR 7 to EUR 27.6, WPC35 from about EUR 3 to EUR 4.3. The slide calls it "the strongest period of price inflation on record", with WPC80 and WPI up about fourfold on 2023 and the sharpest rise in H1 2026: "Demand continues to exceed available WPI and WPC80 production capacity, resulting in the strongest period of price inflation on record." [00:00] (photo 4)

The brand response: fewer promotions, 1 kg packs cut to 900 g at the same price, some reformulation, a rush of new whey launches, and a push to sell higher-margin lines. He believes protein will "look quite differently in 18 to 20 months" [00:00].

Consumer prices per kilogram for priority brands in Europe, October 2025 to October 2026: clear whey up 13.6% (EUR 60.14 to 68.32), HWP/WPI 28.0% (47.73 to 61.10), whey blends 28.8% (37.56 to 48.38), whey hybrids 15.0% (35.64 to 40.97), WPC 20.8% (36.66 to 44.29). From the stage he said 15 to 25 percent [00:00] (photo 8).

The mitigation ladder: price increases (widespread), reduced promotion (increasingly common) and pack architecture (widely adopted globally) are tactical; reformulation is strategic and brand specific; new products and a portfolio shift into creatine, energy and fibre are the top priority, limited by a ground-zero revenue base, brand permission and the risk of alienating core consumers (photo 6).

Whey milkshakes are whey plus milk; whey plus collagen is typically 10 g plus 10 g, in shakes and clear drinks. GLP-1 and longevity proteins, yeast, mycelium and protein from air are coming through but are still expensive [00:00]. "We have never seen more whey hybrids launched in the last 12 months than ever before. It is a fundamental product pillar." [00:00] The slide's examples: Bulk Daily Whey Protein ("best value protein"), Myprotein's Impact Whey Protein Milkshake (20 g protein, 2.6 g sugar, 1.2 g fat per 29 g serving), Clean Simple Eats Protein Powder + Collagen and Planta (20 g protein, 24 vitamins and minerals, 1,000 mg BCAAs) (photo 9).

The six pillars of innovation: whey choice risks confusing consumers; communications react more than they solve; hybrid powders are gaining consistency (dairy plus plant in overt blends); caseinate is the new milkshake; plant protein still needs a taste breakthrough; the Myprotein x Nero launch signals a race for the next cafe collaboration [00:00] (photo 12).

Plant: ranges come in and out; dairy plus plant hybrids are appearing for the first time; caseinates are gaining with milk volatility [00:00]. "What it really wants to say is we're just a really bloody good protein. That is the ideal. By differentiating yourself as being plant, typically lends people to assume it doesn't taste as good." [00:00]

Rocka's vegan range: Pro Protein, 24 g protein, 122 kcal, 83% fava bean and pea, EUR 37.99 per 700 g (EUR 1.65 a serve); Natural Protein, 21 g, 112 kcal, 86.6% soy, fava, almond and pea, EUR 29.99 per 600 g (EUR 1.50 a serve); Protein Shake, "the tastiest vegan protein powder", 84% blend, EUR 37.99 per 900 g (EUR 1.27 a serve). Plant is moving "from an extended product proposition to a simple product attribute" (photo 10).

The creatine benchmark is Optimum Nutrition's Micronised Creatine Powder: 3 g creatine monohydrate a serve, GBP 14.00 for 187 g unflavoured (25p a serve, EUR 0.33) and GBP 16.00 for 247 g flavoured (29p a serve), fronted by Lauren James, Chelsea and England footballer (photo 13).

Creatine formats across 2,639 products: powder 70.1% (13.1% added in the last six months), capsule 17.0% (8.7%), gummy 8.0% (36.2%), tablet 4.2% (14.4%), effervescent 0.4% (10.0%), other 0.3% (44.4%); 378 products, 14.3% of the total, were added in six months (photo 14). "Other" (liquids, foods, chocolate) grew fastest off a tiny base, and most brands now have a route into broader retail [25:59]. Examples: Creatonics' "Creatine+ formulated for women" sachet and Sunday Natural's Nutrachoc creatine chocolate, 20 pieces at 1,000 mg creatine monohydrate, sweetened with tagatose (photo 14) (photo 15).

Hydration: no agreed electrolyte dose (SiS "all five essential", LMNT 1,000 mg sodium, Precision by sweat rate); Liquid IV is the category leader at £1.50 a stick; effervescents are three times cheaper than a stick pack [00:00]. Shelf prices: Liquid I.V. GBP 1.50 a sachet (GBP 9.00 for 6; GBP 1.00 on Clubcard), Phizz GBP 0.40 a tablet (GBP 8.00 for 20; GBP 0.28 on Clubcard), Evian 750 ml GBP 1.85, Red Bull 250 ml GBP 2.10, Lucozade Sport 500 ml GBP 1.65, each single (photo 16).

Declared sodium a serve on selected electrolyte powders: 38 mg (ViDrate Boost), 350 mg (SiS Hydro+), 500 mg (Cadence Daily), 570 mg (Liquid I.V. Multiplier), 750 mg (Hunter & Gather), 1,000 mg (LMNT). 69% of powders include four or five electrolytes; 8% claim Himalayan sea salt as a natural sodium source. The slide: "there is no optimal formula" [00:00] (photo 18).

Hydration powders are positioned three ways: everyday (Humantra, Hunter & Gather, Repowr: routine, natural, sugar-free), superior (SOS "4x faster than water", Ancient + Brave, ARTAH "cellular hydration") and performance (226ERS Hydra Zero on sweat losses, HIGH5 Isotonic carbs plus electrolytes, Precision PH strength options) (photo 22).

Naturalness: 40% state natural colours, 46% use natural flavours, 43% include stevia. Humantra names grape skin as its colour source, Liquid I.V. declares sugar alongside steviol glycosides, ViDrate covers flavour, colour and sweetening in one proposition, Cadence extends the absence message to fillers [00:00] (photo 24).

Tracked listings (US and Europe, 16,412 across eight spaces): creatine 3,448 (new-product activity +10% over the latest six months), magnesium 2,833 (+15%), collagen 2,648, energy and focus 2,153, pre-workout 1,869, sleep and mood 1,626, electrolyte 1,487, longevity 348 (+20% new). From the stage: almost 3,500 creatine, almost 2,800 magnesium, over 2,500 collagen. "Only a few will be really successful" [00:00] (photo 23).

Branded ingredient penetration (share of tracked products with at least one identified branded ingredient): pre-workout 53% (many use more than one), longevity 40%, energy and focus 31%, sleep and mood 25%, creatine 25%, collagen 25%, electrolyte 17%, magnesium 17%. The slide adds that minerals in general are "needing to work harder to prove the benefit" [18:50] (photo 27).

Longevity takes three approaches: alter the ageing process (cellular health, mitochondria, senescence), optimise the ageing experience (muscle and mobility, cognition, energy, sleep) or personalise to a life stage (ageing athletes, menopause, later life). Example: Cellaro's Vitalize AM, Renew PM and Reset monthly range against the 12 hallmarks of ageing [18:50] (photo 29).

Longevity and athlete-backed brands compete for the same consumer: Sergio Ramos links sport to longevity through Centenarian ("Real longevity, backed by science. To perform better. To live better."), with normal sports products framed as living better today. The competitive set has never been broader [18:50] (photo 30).

Brands should engage with gut and microbiome, longevity and GLP-1, but stay true to the industry's DNA; this will be "the biggest challenge you face for your budgets and strategy in 2027 and beyond" [18:50].

The four closing principles: think beyond the category (new consumers, needs and occasions); stay true to your DNA (capabilities, credibility, differentiation); choose where to compete ("where you could play from where you should play"); know your right to win (where you can create distinctive value). "Growth creates opportunity. Understanding change creates advantage." [18:50] (photo 32)

takeaways.text: Starbucks' 15 g protein cold foam is his example of the bigger market: Starbucks say one in seven coffees now provides 15 g of protein. A bigger market is not more of the same market [00:00].

Brands are not just mitigating whey prices but going through a "structural reset". New products that cut whey reliance and a shift into creatine, energy and fibre are the "top priority for brands" [00:00] (photo 6).

More "whey hybrids" (sold as whey, blended with milk, soy or yeast to cut cost) launched in the last 12 months than ever; whey milkshakes and whey plus collagen are the next pillars [00:00] (photo 9).
Plant protein still underdelivers on taste. It should sell itself as a very good protein, not as plant [00:00] (photo 10).
Gummies are the fastest-growing creatine format by new launches: 8.0% of creatine products, 36.2% of them added in the last six months, with "lots of conjecture about stability" [00:00] (photo 14).

"Creatine, which is my benchmark, one in four products uses a branded ingredient. It wouldn't take you a genius to work out where most of that comes from. There's a race for those to follow, by the way." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [18:50]
"The growth is good, and it creates opportunity. You all have a seat at the table, but it doesn't mean to say you're all going to win." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [18:50]

# Unfiltered: An Insider's View of the Whey Protein Market: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Alan Johnstone - SNS - whey pricing", https://otter.ai/u/3wuSdbgu4ue-m20dOaERZG2gsKY, recorded 9 Nov 2026 09:36, 17m 15s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Speaker 1: To deal with it, we've got Alan Johnston, owner of Nutrilution.
[00:16] Speaker 2: I'm going to talk about wafers here. For those who don't know me, I've spent most of the last decades selling whey protein. First at Sarawak International, and then more recently at Arla Foods Ingredients. And so, hopefully, I'm qualified to talk about this. The purpose, really, of this presentation is to give you a better understanding of what happens in the supply chain for whey protein. We're fairly familiar with the consumer side, and that's with the intention that you can understand the restrictions on whey protein manufacturers, but also you can understand some of the decisions they might make over the next few years. Nutrition, as Nikki says, is my new business. We also sell nutritional ingredients, mostly more niche, higher value ingredients, but we can also help buyers with sourcing strategy for whey proteins and dairy proteins generally, especially if you're looking to set up cross continental supply chains. So, if that sounds interesting, then do talk to me afterwards. This slide illustrates nicely why you want this on the agenda. So WPI is the top line on the graph here, rising from around seven euros a kilogram back in 2023, all the way up to over 30 euros per kilogram earlier this year, with very little respite in that curve for buyers. WPCAT actually pretty stable, and I would argue quite good value for most of that time, until earlier this year when the price rocketed from 12 euros per kilogram all the way up to 28 in the space for about six weeks, and it was that sudden increase that put so much pressure on brands and the industry, partly because of the speed, because of course they have no time at all to react, and partly because businesses had already switched their sourcing away from WPI and into WPC80, and that meant that the WPC80 price was more of an existential risk for brands, as opposed to the WPI price, which was more of a break on the Profitability. So we're going to have a little look at why that's happened. Really quick on demand. Nick's covered all of this really, but and traditional sports nutrition grown extremely fast. Urine monitor staying 10% a year. I think most people I know see that as a big underestimate. Probably growing faster than that, GLP-1 again, no secret here. You've got a huge number of adults taking this and spending a lot more money on protein supplements than they had previously. And of course, these are people who weren't necessarily in the gym before, so they probably weren't buying protein supplements before. And this is incremental demand. That's plus protein more mainstream. I've also used the Starbucks example. You could choose Papa John's pizza. You could choose Dunkin' Donuts. It's just just everywhere. And then I've plucked out Clearway as a sub trend. Now, partly because it didn't really exist five years ago, so this is now one of the fastest selling parts of the category, and partly because it is almost all whey, so it has a disproportionate effect on the supply chain for whey proteins. Most of these trends would support all protein sources, and they especially source whey protein because, for most purposes, whey protein is the best protein source. It's nutritionally superior in terms of muscle protein synthesis. Don't mind a debate on whether your average consumer really benefits much from that. You know they probably don't. And in fact, certainly the more mainstream you get with protein products, the less people care about the protein source. I think what people always care about is taste and texture. And whey protein is delicious. It is light. It's smooth. It mixes easily. It's just far easier for a business to create a good-tasting whey protein product with whey than it is with most of the alternative protein sources. Hence the surge in demand. Moving to supply, starting the bottom left here, kind of the composition of milk. want to call out that only 0.6 liquid milk is whey protein, and that's important to understand the production process, but also the decisions that whey protein producers take. Because of course, a high whey protein price doesn't necessarily make for a happy dairy farming. You're also going to be able to sell and get value for all of these other elements of the liquid milk as well. In order to get whey protein from that, you start by making cheese. You don't have to. There are other ways of whey protein. Life are the most common. Start with cheese production, and the cheese keeps the casein protein and it keeps most of the fat, and then you end up with liquid whey, which is around 12% protein by dry matter. From there, if you want to get to WPCA, so you go through ultrafiltration, so you're filtering off the minerals, you're filtering off a lot of lactose, like that. But if you want to go to WPR, you go through microfiltration, another production process, and that is where you filter off the remaining fats. But unfortunately, with that fat, you also lose quite a lot of your protein. Then, if you want to add even more value, you want to go to clear whey or you want to go to hydrolyzed whey protein, then you go through yet another production process. And it's these production processes that are one of the first bottlenecks for whey protein supply. These factories are phenomenally expensive, and they take a long time to build. So, if you're a whey protein producer, you're making really big bets a long way in advance, and then you've got to be really confident of your business case in order to do that. And a huge part of your business case is: Can you source enough whey to fill that factory up? So this is the second bottleneck, arguably the most important one, which is that cheese production is only growing around one and a half percent a year, and that means that liquid whey production is only growing around one and a half percent a year. You can, of course, source whey protein from other areas, so you can try and find a cheese factory that wasn't already selling it. You could take whey away from another whey derivative like sweet whey powder or WPC 35, and businesses are doing that. But there's a limit to how much you can do that. Ultimately, you come up against this bottleneck. It's probably the most important conclusion from the presentation already, really, which is that cheese is only growing one and a half percent a year, whereas waferaging demand is growing whatever figure we choose over over 10%. Byproducts are then another limitation on how fast this can grow because you can't only sell the wafers; you've got to sell the byproducts as well. If you're making WPC 80, you're only left with permeate and lactose, which fairly easy to get rid of. If you're making WPI, you've also then got to sell this fatty protein stream, and these byproducts complicate the business cases because if you think that whey protein manufacturers are essentially competing to buy what limited liquid whey is available, the people who can afford to pay the most for the liquid whey are the businesses that can add the most value to them, and that's not just the protein itself; it's also all these byproducts. So, in the way that's played out over the last five years, looks a bit like this. So, you've got total whey protein supply growing just under 5%. Okay, go. So you can see that there's clearly whey being reprioritized away from lower value derivatives into high protein. Within that, then you've got WPI growing a lot faster than WPC8. If you think back to that first graph I showed you with the WPI graph rising higher and earlier, you can understand why producers have prioritized WPI manufacturing capacity. Of course, that's come at the expense of WPC 80 because you can funnel as much weight as you possibly can into WPI production, which it also helps to explain why WPC80 was so undersupplied earlier this year. You might ask, well, if WPI has been growing 15% year on year, why was it so expensive? It's partly because, of course, demand's been growing so fast. It's also because I mentioned the Clearway trend earlier, and a lot of that WPI chunk is now Clearway, and it wasn't five years ago. Estimates vary on what percentage of the WPI market is Clearway. I've used 25% here, which is right at the top of the estimate range. It's probably a little bit below that, but it illustrates that actually the the instant WPI, the normal WPI that you're used to using in the past has been growing much more slowly, more like eight and a half percent a year, and that is below the underlying category level. Looking to the future, so on the left there you've got American manufacturing increases over the next couple of years. This is quite good data. Each one of those little blocks represents a different supplier, so it's quite granular and should be fairly accurate. On the right, I've got European production increases. I've got a lot less detail here, so I've got some names. What they're going to be making. In fact, that's not even an exhaustive list. There's a few manufacturers in Eastern Europe that just can't really get information out of, but the headline is you'd expect WPI to be growing around between seven and 11% a year, WPC 80 a bit slower, four to 7% a year, but both of those figures can't be at the upper estimate. So if WPI is growing 11% a year, then WPC 80 has to be more like four because there's not enough whey. So, with both those figures being relatively modest, you'd argue below the underlying demand for protein. Should we just expect whey protein to become ever more expensive over time? Well, not necessarily, because you've also got a lot of behavior in here. I've used the COVID period here to illustrate a point. It's quite an extreme period, of course, but it does a good job of making this point. If we looked at that graph, you'd expect either supply or demand or both to have been absolutely all over the place. Of course, in reality, they weren't. Both are growing, but they're just growing at different rates. What's really going on here is when COVID hit, buyers stopped buying, which is a fair enough response to uncertainty. So of course the stock levels depleted, and consumers keep buying whey protein products, and they keep probably buying them faster than ever. But at the same time, the supply chain starts to break down. So you've got truck drivers not able to drive. You've got container ships getting stuck at port, and the logistics network just can't keep up with these orders. So if you're a buyer, you're not only trying to replenish the stock that you depleted, you're not only trying to meet increased consumer demand, you're also trying to build extra stocks to allow for a longer lead time. If your lead time has gone from three months to six months, then you need a lot more stock. And because of that, production then can't keep up. So if you're a whey protein supplier, you can't meet all of this extra demand in a short period of time. And so now buyers are competing to be the ones to buy available whey proteins, which means the price goes up. Because the price goes up, buyers are incentivised to buy as early as possible to get the best price. That adds even more to short-term demand, so the price goes up again, and you're into this this vicious cycle. The opposite is also true. So then, looking forward to a time when truck drivers are back on the roads, container ships moving again. All of this, all of these orders, all of this, this demand starts to arrive at warehouses. So inventories grow, and lead times are now shorter. Maybe in the meantime, businesses have taken steps to reduce their usage because of the prices. So they've increased consumer pricing. They've reformulated. They've reduced pack sizes, and now buyers are sitting on quite a lot of stock that they don't really need. So they might say, "Well, I can afford not to buy for a month or two months or whatever it is." Now the stock's growing at the producer level, which means that we're competing to sell. That pushes the price down because the price is falling. Now buyers want to wait as long as they possibly can before they arrive. That pushes demand down even further. Then again, you're back into this this flywheel, and that's a really good example of where we are now. So over the last few weeks, WPC80 has been falling pretty hard. WPI still expensive, but definitely correcting. And this is a direct response to pricing getting so high so fast earlier in the year. Brands have taken all these steps to reduce their usage. In the meantime, you've got a few new factories in commissions in America. So finally, factories that were were probably set in motion three or four years ago when these prices started to go up are finally coming to production, and then there's enough stock to go around so buyers can stock up, and and now they don't need all this extra inventory. So WPAT80 prices is coming down fast. On the other hand, all of the alternatives for things you can do with your whey are expensive. So WPI is still expensive, even WPC 35 is expensive. Even sweet whey powder is now quite a good product to manufacture if you're a producer. So they've got options for what to do with their whey, and that means you'd expect to see WPC 80 production reduce probably quite sharply. Well, right now, but then in the next couple of months as well. Added to that, the alternative proteins that brands have substituted into their formulations are going up in price. So I've used MPC 85 here. You know, you could pick MPI, you can pick caseins, you can pick plant proteins. Really, those two lines, the yellow and the blue line, should never meet. WPC80 should always be more expensive than milk protein. Of course, markets do this. You know the quote from Keane saying that markets can remain irrational for longer than you can remain solvent, so it's it's worth considering that you know just because those lines touch doesn't mean they suddenly bounce away from each other, but it can't go on forever. You'd expect at some stage these these things to correct. So then, looking a little bit ahead, I've used here a deliberately vague graph, so that line is a bit of a blend of WPC80 and WPI price over the last few years, taking all the pricing off, taking most of the timings off because, as I say, it's impossible to be precise with these things. But the way I see the market is, you've got the whey protein price over time rising because demand for proteins, we saw as these many drivers, it's pretty strong. Then you've got a limitation in terms of the speed of liquid whey production. So the price goes up over time, but then the actual price can get quite a long way from what we might consider a balanced price. And you definitely argue that WPCAD did that recently. When it does that, you get these overcorrections driven by the behaviors we just looked at. But then, at some stage, it always gets dragged back towards that, towards that macro trend. That's probably not especially useful for you because, of course, no one knows what a balanced price should be. No one knows how far away the actual price can get before it starts to get dragged back in line. So my advice, as my conclusion for the the presentation, pretty simple. I think don't try to be too clever with your weight rating volume. If you try and buy right at the bottom of the market and you miss it, then you're left trying to replenish stocks when the price is going up, and that's the worst possible time to be doing it. So, if the price that you're paying right now allows you to make money as a business, then keep buying, keep your inventory steady as you can, and then you won't get caught out. But then also realize that whey protein will be expensive. It should be expensive. It's the best protein source for so many uses. It's got a structural supply restriction, and the amount of protein is not really going away. So, if your business can't cope with the sort of supplies we've seen earlier this year, then you need to change something in your business model. All right, I'm done. Time for some questions.
[17:01] Speaker 1: Any questions from the floor at all? I haven't seen any come in on Slido. So brilliant. I think, in the interest of time, we'll move straight on to the panel. But thank you so much, Alan. That was really useful.

summary.Summary:
Alan Johnstone, who has spent most of the last decades selling whey protein, most recently at Arla Foods Ingredients, and now runs Nutrilution, explained why whey prices hit records this year and what buyers should do about it.

His answer starts with milk. Whey protein comes from cheese, and cheese production grows only about one and a half percent a year, while demand for whey protein grows by 10% or more: sports nutrition, GLP-1 users, protein in everyday food, and clear whey. Filtration plants are expensive and take years to build, and producers have put the whey they have into isolate, so concentrate was short when brands had just switched to it.

Prices then swing further than supply and demand alone would explain, because buyers stock up when prices rise and wait when they fall. That is happening now: concentrate is falling fast, isolate is correcting, and the proteins brands moved into are rising.

His advice was plain. Do not try to time the bottom. Keep buying steadily if today's price lets you make money. And accept that whey will stay expensive, because the supply limit is structural.

Transcribed by Claude from the photo; the photo is the original. Alan Johnstone, Nutrilution, SANS Europe, 9 Nov 2026.
--- photo 4 ---
How whey protein is made, and why there's so little of it (slide 4)
The production journey: from raw milk to refined whey protein. Raw milk (~3.4% protein) -> coagulation (rennet) -> Cheese (the primary product) -> whey drained off -> Liquid whey (co-product of cheese) -> ultrafiltration + drying -> WPC (35-80% protein) -> microfiltration / ion exchange -> WPI (>=90% protein) -> acidify or hydrolyse -> Clear / Hydrolysed WPI (>=90%, refined).
What's in milk (by weight): Water 87.3%; Lactose 4.7%; Fat 3.9%; Casein 2.8%; Minerals 0.7%; Whey 0.6% (whey protein).
Other Whey Derivatives. Beyond protein, there are other options and by-products for producers: Sweet whey powder (~12% protein); Whey permeate (lactose + minerals); Lactose (purified milk sugar); Demineralised whey (D70 / D90, infant nutrition); Procream / WFC (whey cream / fat).
Source: typical cow's-milk composition & dairy processing, indicative industry figures.
