Okay, let's bit of a history lesson. Let's sort of set the stage, set the context for talking about GLP-1. So, as you might imagine I've been doing this presentation quite a lot, speaking about GRP one, often to the kind of food and drink sector. And if we look at the kind of last 50 years, it's actually been in the round quite a good time in the food and drink sector. And this is for a few reasons. First of all, as you can see, the population has been growing. So this is we just look at the UK, just just illustratively, but the population has been growing. So, as a food and drink business or as a nutrition business, you've had more people you can sell to. You've then also had more people consuming more things, consuming more calories. So, per person and at a population level, more people consuming more things, and then even adjusting for inflation, you've still got more people spending more, so more people consuming more products and spending more on them. That's pretty good context from a market perspective. Put those together, you can kind of see, broadly speaking, the line goes up. If you also add into the mix that we're obviously in a bit of a cost of living crisis, and to a lesser extent we're in sort of entering a bit of a population crisis, sort of those three lines that we're all going up start to be a bit more of question and start to be a bit more dramatic. Now the thing is, when I do this presentation for food and drink brands, this is the part of the presentation where I have to say, and now for the bad news. However, in this room, this is the opposite story. This is actually the fun part of the job, where I can actually say this is a real opportunity for you, and we'll come on to unpack why. Now, GLP-1 is, you know, as we as we saw from the kind of show of thumbs at the start, this is an issue which is still not super well known, super well understood, and it's also an issue which I think a lot of people think is quite horizontal. They think this is an issue that is that is coming down the line. And like I say, I'm still just the next two or three slides will still just be looking at UK data before we look at European wide data. What I should say is, is if you look at those percentages, we did a study over the summer, and we actually saw similar use of current usage of GLP-1 in Italy, France, Germany, and Spain. So this is actually an issue and a concept which is becoming as prevalent on the continent as it is in the UK, and obviously the US is a bit further ahead. But what I really wanted to stress here is that this is an issue which is live now. So, 6.1% of the UK population are currently taking GLP-1s. 5.7% of the population have previously used GLP-1s, and 15.1% of the population are considering using them. summary.Summary:
Morgan Griffiths of Lumina Intelligence argued that GLP-1 drugs, bad news for many food and drink brands, are an opportunity for active nutrition.

He started with scale. In the UK, 6.1% of people are taking a GLP-1 now, and with past users and those considering it the total is about 18.4 million people. Use is similar in Italy, France, Germany and Spain.

He then described the users. They are not the obesity population the drugs were designed for: most are women, Gen X or Millennial and better off. They are already health-minded and willing to pay more for quality. Most expect to spend the same or more on food and drink, and near 60% expect to take more supplements, with creatine higher on the list than he expected.

He saw three openings: side effects, nutrition gaps such as protein intake and muscle loss, and lapsed users, who risk regaining the weight because the drug changed their behaviour without them changing their habits. Huel, Cambridge Nutrition, Portion IQ and Boots are already moving, and Lumina forecasts UK use at around 11% by 2031.

Morgan Griffiths presents an analysis of the growing GLP-1 consumer market and its significant commercial opportunities for the food and drink sector.

## Market Context
**Morgan** provides a statistical overview of the current GLP-1 landscape, emphasizing that it is a live issue rather than a future trend. In the UK, 6.1% of the population currently uses **GLP-1**, 5.7% have used it previously, and 15.1% are considering it. This cohort represents approximately 18.4 million people, making the group larger than the combined vegan and vegetarian populations in the UK.

**Key demographic findings:**
*   Users are predominantly female (56%).
*   The age profile consists mostly of Gen X or Millennials (63%).
*   Most users belong to higher socio-economic groups (63% are ABC1).
*   The consumer base is health-minded, values quality, and is willing to pay more for functional benefits.

## Consumer Behavior
Despite concerns regarding reduced food volume consumption, **Morgan** notes that roughly two-thirds of users spend either the same or more on food and drink compared to before starting treatment. Many users also increase their use of supplements, with nearly 90% maintaining or increasing usage.

**Innovation opportunities include:**
*   Addressing side effects such as nausea and reduced food enjoyment through specialized products.
*   Tackling nutritional gaps caused by lower calorie intake, specifically regarding protein intake and muscle loss prevention.
*   Providing support for "lapsed users" who face a high risk—four times higher than traditional methods—of regaining weight once medication is stopped due to unchanged behaviors.

## Industry Response
Current market players are already pivoting toward this demographic through targeted product innovation and retail positioning. Examples of existing industry movement include:

*   **Huel**: Moving into blended nutrition/supplement spaces with low-calorie versions of existing products.
*   **Cambridge Nutrition** and **Portion IQ**: Developing specialized beverages, snacks, and meal replacements for **GLP-1** users.
*   **Boots**: Implementing dedicated retail bays and shelf signage that addresses specific side effects like hair or skin issues associated with medication use.

[00:15] Speaker 2 (Gulrez Zariwala): Thank you, Morgan, for setting the scene, and thanks to Native Ingredients for having me here. I'd like to start by a very brief introduction. My background is in drug delivery and formulation science. Also, have background in obesity and metabolism. I'm currently the founder director of the Center for Nutraceuticals, and I just like take a couple of minutes to talk a bit about our work because our clinicals and all our research is based at the center, so it's a first of a kind initiative. One of objectives to add to the bridge between industry and academia to bring some credibility, independent research-based opinions. We're based in central London. That's us. That's not all of us. That's the BD Tower. It's just us on the the fourth floor of the building. Just make that clear. Okay, so we work in a range of disciplines from sports and exercise all the way to nutrition, metabolism, neurobiology, formulation science. We have quite a multidisciplinary team, and our research model is also quite vertically integrated. We work on the mechanistic side all the way to the clinical side. We work with developing formulation strategies for novel as well as existing molecules. We then carry out mechanistic studies to test them using the relevant cell lines. This then feeds into human intervention studies, which can be sponsored by the industry or they are open sky, blue blue sky, open-ended research. This may inform product development, which we have also worked on quite a bit. So, just to give you a bit of breadth of our work, there's a recent publications all the way from sports, exercise, nutrition. There's a lot of curcumin-based work. We did some quite pioneering clinical trials about five, six years back, and all the way to obesity and metabolism, which I'm going to talk about. We work with partners across the world, from UK SMEs to large companies, and we collaborate with a number of universities as well as advising governments on nutraceutical and supplement-related policies. Today, I'm going to focus on clinical trials we have done. Again, as I said, we are very much research-founded. It's all about conducting research, publishing papers, but we actually work with the industry because our objective is to bring the science as much as possible. So let's come to the topic at hand. Obesity is an academic. We know it's a public health crisis. The prevalence is quite widespread. These are the hotspots, as you can see, in developed as well as emerging economies, particularly let's say U.S., the incidence is high at 40%. Equally, you have the same in South America as well as some parts of Africa, almost 35 to 40%. So obesity is chronic and multifactorial. It would be hard to simplify it within the remit of this talk. You have socioeconomic factors, psychological factors, genetic factors. All of these come in play, and you have a lot of secondary diseases related to obesity. These may be metabolic as well as non-metabolic. Metabolic type two diabetes, non-metabolic neurodegeneration, dementia, all strongly correlated to obesity. Obesity is generally quite simplistically defined as BMI over 30. Now we know there are more complex measures and screening tools. BMI is the consensus. It's a very simple ratio of height and weight, and it's quite widely used. So it's over 30, which is defined as obesity, and you have lower cutoff for say overweight. You have higher cutoff for type one, type two, type three obesity. Quite simply, it may not be the best picture, but it's it's the wave balance at the bottom. It is energy imbalance. You're intaking excess energy in terms of calories than what your energy expenditure is. If you get that right, you have a lean body. If there is any kind of alteration due to the various factors, you're prone to obesity. So, talking about silver bullets and magic bullets, there's long been a surge all the way from the 20s and 30s. You have some quite questionable material there. Let's talk about in the next slide. These were called rainbow pills. But over time, the most kind of desirable approach has always been diet and exercise. A diet low in calories, high in protein, high in fiber, balanced in carbs, and low in fat is ideal. However, it is not practical and as feasible as we might want it to be. So then we have bariatric surgery, gastric banding, and so on. This is most effective and durable treatment. This is applicable to certain populations and carries its own risks and costs. We then have pharmacological approaches. We are going to talk about GLP ones. Again, these are quite beneficial to certain populations, as we know, but they require lifelong use and the risk profile is quite low at the minute, but there there is some potential. There are some studies to show some adverse effects, which we'll touch upon. So let's look at a brief history of obesity drugs before we go into supplements. Now, as you can see, there's long been a search for the silver bullet, and this has really been marked by failures, all the way from the 20s, where you had the rainbow pills. This was a cocktail of antidepressant diuretics and all sort of questionable drugs, thyroid extract, and then coming all the way to the GLPs, all the drugs marked in red were withdrawn, with the exception of olistat, which is a fat blocker acts on lipoprotein lipase. Most of them are centrally acting, meaning they act on the brain. So the issue with centrally acting drugs is highlighted by rimonaban, which was the most recently withdrawn drug. It acts on the endocannabinoid receptors, endocannabinoid system. It did have quite potent effects on reducing appetite, on weight loss. However, these centers in the brain are quite tightly wired to your centers of pleasure, your heteronistic centers, and any kind of tinkering which lead to an imbalance, which is what you can see here. There's a very high incidence of neuropsychiatric effects all the way to it being a suicide risk. So this was withdrawn, and this directed the focus to peripheral therapies, which is gut hormone-based approaches. So what are gut hormones? The gastrointestinal tract, GI tract, is interestingly one of the largest endocrine organ of the body. It has specialized cells both in the small intestine all the way to the large intestine. Now these are L cells, and they respond to dietary stimulus, different components of diet, qualitatively and quantitatively. Again, protein, carbs, fats. They will respond according to the let's say the proportion, the quality, in response to that, there will be a secretion of gut hormones, which will then signal directly and indirectly to the brain, and this will balance out to create your feeling of hunger or satiety. It's not just the gut which is secreting hormones. You have them coming from the pancreas. You have them coming from fat tissue. Focusing on the gut hormones, we have them coming from secreted from the stomach, from the small intestine, all the way to the large intestine. These are ghrelin, GLP-1, PYY, oxymodulin, GIP. Other than ghrelin, which gives a positive signal, it makes you feel hungry. So between meals, when your stomach is shrinking, ghrelin is secreted, goes to the brain, signals, makes you feel hungry. All the others give a negative signal to the brain, particularly PYY and GLP-1. So interestingly, it's PYY peptide YY, which is the more potent anorexigenic hormone, which causes you to eat less. But due to a combination of commercial and clinical reasons, it's the GLPs, which very came in first as a class. Let's talk about GLP-1. It's an incretin hormone. It's released directly in response to dietary intake of certain components of food, let's say protein, following its release, it will be secreted in blood, and it will act on the organs surrounding it. So it will go to the pancreas, cause it to release insulin, maintain insulin balance. It will go to the pancreas, cause the glucagon to go down, it will also signal to the brain directly and indirectly, directly through the local nerves and indirectly going through the bloodstream across the blood-brain barrier and signaling to the GLP-1 receptors to cause you to eat less. Now the issue with the GLP-1 as a molecule was that it's rapidly degraded in your body by the enzyme DPP4, and this frustrated attempts to develop therapeutics for for quite a long time. And the solution was until the answer was found in in this reptile. I think the people from North America might be familiar. So it's the the Gila monster. I think it's pronounced with the H, although it's G. So this is some classic blue sky research, curiosity-driven research, where the researchers observe that it eats only five to 10 times a day, and sorry, a year, and it has a very good metabolic profile. So there was a search for hormones within it, and it was found to be exendin four, which is a long-acting LP1 analog. This led to patenting by a researcher. Pharmaceutical companies were not interested. Ultimately, Emilin acquired it. This became BioTuff, short-acting, first of its class. It then went on to the longer-acting drugs, from once a day to once a week, and then we have the latest, which is once a week, and these are dual GLP-1 and GIP acting drugs. Okay, this is just because of structural modifications. You increase the resilience to DPP-4, stays longer in your body, creates the effects that you want. Some of them are available as oral pills as well, and there are other small molecules now which are again available as pills. So, because of these dramatic weight loss effects, as you can see, between five to 15%, you have the transition of a highly regulated prescription drug to become almost a lifestyle product, as was touched upon in the previous talk. This is due to a number of complex factors. Again, we can spend an entire talk on that. There's a ease of availability through digital pharmacies. There are cosmetic pressures, and again, there are some cost reductions compared to what it was originally. LP1 also. has quite a important role in sports nutrition, both in people who are elite athletes as well as educational athletes have noticed that there is reduction in inflammation. There's increased energy levels. There are mechanisms to to support this. Again, it has benefits in sports such as Marshall Sports, where tight cut-offs are required, and as you can imagine, it's it's not banned yet, but it's on the watch list for for this reason. The last point, again, it's been covered in depth in in the previous talk. It leads to good supplementation with a number of other supplements in in other categories. So just like all drugs, there's a balance between benefits and risks, and there is a side effect profile. So these are not all adverse effects occurring in all consumers and users. But these have been reported. The most prominent ones are the GI side effects, nausea vomiting. There are some cosmetic effects, such as when you lose the buckle, the facial fat pads, also the breakdown in collagen, so you have the sucking skin, and importantly, all GLP-1 based drugs cause a reduction in body weight, not specifically body fat. So you have a reduction in muscle mass, which can lead to sarcopenia. So this directed a lot of consumers to supplement based solutions, and this led to the GLP one boom. This is from Expo West last year, where everybody was talking everything was GLP-1, and there are some products with some scientific basis, but some of them are a bit of a stretch, and there are pitfalls to this. As you can see, there's some high-profile lawsuits, there's some regulatory clampdowns, and ultimately, and importantly, leads to lowering of the consumer confidence. So, are there any supplements that have a scientific basis? Looked at a few of them. Proteins have an undisputed effect on GLP-1 secretion, both mechanistically, animal models, human study. Depends on the quality of the protein. Depends on the amino acid profile. Both supplemental as well as dietary proteins. Just to clarify, so this is one of the 2015 studies: high protein versus high carb versus high fat, 60 to 70 percent in each. And as you can see, a very prominent post meal, significant increase in both GLP-1 and PYY. So again, proteins scientifically validated, and they can also support the muscle loss that occurs to the LP1, so it's got some good credentials as a supplement. Lipid-based compounds, OEA is a molecule produced by a body. It is rapidly degraded. It has direct effects on GPR119, which causes GLP1 secretion. So there's a very direct mechanism. As I said, it's rapidly degraded. So formulation strategies may improve its profile, and you have a molecule called tripty. This has been recently studied. There's a latest paper which shows a dose-dependent increase in post-meal GLP-1 secretion. Berberine, I'm sure everyone here is familiar. It's often referred to as iti. It's alkaloid compound from barberries. So berberine does have some GLP-1 effects, but they are indirect, and a lot of them have been shown in animal models, mainly rodent studies. There are a couple of human studies, but its main effects is on maintaining glucose metabolism in a positive way, maintaining fat balance, and this is through actions on AMPK. On GLP-1, it has indirect effects, and most studies have shown quite modest effects on GLP-1 as well as on weight loss. Cinnamon is often combined with berberine. Cinnamon is rich in cinnamondehyde, cinnamondeide has a mechanistic basis. It acts on the ion channel trip A1, and through that it can increase GLP1 secretion. But it has mild to modest effects, and there are very few human studies to substantiate this. Next, we have beta compounds. So this is a bit of a crossover because bitter compounds include alkaloids, polyphenols can include berberine, which we talked about. There is a mechanistic basis. Bitter compounds is part of your body's natural defense system. They act on the taste receptors, particularly TAS tubar, and through that, which is a G protein-coupled receptor, so mostly it will bring about calcium increase in your cells and kick out protein hormones. It brings about increased secretion of GLP-1, but there have been very few human studies, and again it's a mild to modest effect. So I'm going to talk about some of our primary work on appetite regulation. We've been working on it for about eight to 10 years. We started with a focus on dietary proteins. We did the first study comparing the metabolic profile of plant proteins. We worked with protein, potato protein as well as rice protein, comparing it to whey protein isolate. So until then, most of the work was looking at the anabolic profile. Very few studies had looked at the effect on glucose metabolism. This was quite a complex quadruple crossover study. There's some very interesting results which were published, and I'm proud of it. It featured on the cover page of a journal. But the main objective was to progress this into appetite study, which led us to the appetite study. So this was called appetite. So this is a triple crossover study. We compared the effects of potato protein versus whey protein isolate. Again, one of the first studies comparing plant as well as milk proteins and a placebo-controlled study, so three arms a crossover study. Participants come in on the day of the study, following an overnight fast, and they will consume breakfast. We try to make it as palatable as possible. This is spiked with protein. Okay, so this is isocaloric, isovolimic. So all proteins will be having the same calorie, the same protein content, and the the placebo is also matched to this. Following the consumption, we will connect them to a cannula. We'll draw blood every 30 minutes, and they will also complete an appetite code. Following that, three hours later, they'll have a meal ablibitum, which you can eat as much as you want, and that's a huge bowl of pasta. We try to make it again appetizing, so that doesn't have a confounding factor. So the idea is that if the protein is creating a satiety effect, you're going to eat less, and this is going to be matched by the the peptide hormone release. So it's quite a complex hypothesis, and we wanted to explore this. And interestingly, we got some really exciting results. So, firstly, we showed that both the plant as well as the biprotein analyst, because a significant increase in GLP-1. The second important and novel result is that the equivalent response on GLP-1, as you can see between the teal and the pink in the plant protein compared to the whey protein isolate. Again, it's one of the first times it's been shown. And the third result, which is particularly significant, is that although at 180 minutes post meal, you're not seeing a significant increase in in GIP. Whey protein is leading to a significant increase in GIP at 60 minutes. So GIP acts in a different way to GLP-1. It may act more instantly and directly on appetite as compared to GLP-1. So it makes sense to combine them. This is why you have the new class of pharmaceutical drugs, which are a combination of GLP and GIS on others. This is the first nutraceutical compound, whey protein isolate, which shows a similar effect, not to the same magnitude, but the same trend. So the next study was on botanical. This is just completed last month, and hopefully we will submit it for publication next week. We're very excited about it. The last study you saw was independent study, unfunded, conducted as part of a PhD project. We do a lot of studies which are industry sponsored, but there's a balance between the academic work we do and the sponsored work. So we try to feed in from our academic research into this. So this is a replicate of our academic study. This study was done with support from Finova. It's a UK-based company, and the molecule is called Redicools. Redi Cools is a standardized mulberry extract. It is available across the world. It's used in a number of finished products as an ingredient, combined with other ingredients as well. It has a number of studies showing it to have effect on glucose metabolism. Quite simply, it limits, it slows down the absorption of carbohydrates, prevents sugar spikes. The hypothesis is for us, if it's slowing down the absorption of carbs in the small intestine, they are likely to go in the large intestine, where through generation of short chain fatty acids, there should be hypothetically an effect on GLP-1, which is what we want to test out. So it's a triple crossover study. One arm was the placebo, the second was the radicos formulation, the third is a combination of radicos with two other compounds, and this is one of the leading U.S. GLP-1 brands, which we brought in the study, also funded. So we often do studies where we look at combination effects of supplements because it's easy to show isolated effects with one ingredient and so on, and you want to show a true effect of a finished product. You want to see if the ingredients are working in synergy. So that's why it was important for us to have this as an arm. Study design was similar to a previous study. We recruited in central London, so very much centralized as compared to a lot of trials which are decentralized these days. We like to do blood work through blood collections through cannulation in house. Also, we like to focus on having a diverse multi ethnic population with a good balance of female as well as male participants, as you can see. And the BMI cutoff is also relevant to the actual consumer. So the study is designed with the consumer in mind, not just an idealized population. Similar to the previous study, we had the participants coming in, taking the pill, consuming the breakfast. They filled appetite scores for three hours. Then every 30 minutes, we were collecting the the blood samples, and then they completed another questionnaire over 24 hours, which is called a food noise questionnaire, which I'm going to talk about, Muradal. So we didn't really know what to expect from this study because this kind of work hadn't been done before, even mechanistically. The results were quite exciting. So we saw the response of both the ingredient and the formulation on glucose response, which we expected. What we also saw was a statistically significant increase in GLP-1 secretion post meal at 180 minutes. Matched by that, we also saw a significant reduction in appetite. However, what is most interesting for us was a significant reduction in food noise. So, for those who are familiar, food noise is intrusive thoughts related to food, and these are often related to food cravings, binge eating, overeating, and so on. A lot of the the GLP-1 trials carried out food noise questionnaires. There's strong food noise data. This is one of the first supplemental nutraceutical studies that used food noise as an endpoint. The 24 hours following the supplementation intervention, we saw a significant reduction. That is 21, 19 to 21, 19 with one and 21 with the other, reduction in food noise. So a significant increase in GLP-1, increase sorry reduction in appetite and reduction in food noise. Hopefully, we're going to continue this study. We want to do it long term. If the industry partner supports, we'd like to see effect. We would like to explore effect on body weight composition as well. And hopefully, in 2728, we'll be carrying out two follow on studies with this molecule as well as the the finished product. So, just a quick summary of the key points from my perspective: GLP-1 drugs have transformed our approach to to obesity and appetite regulation. They provide dramatic effects. At present, the side effect profile is is quite favorable. It's it's not particularly negative, but they do carry the risk which needs to be recognized because ultimately it is it is a drug. It's a pharmacological drug. Supplements and nutritional and nutraceutical interventions may fill a gap, either with active users concurrently or with lapsed users. However, there needs to be some management of expectation. There is no natural supplement solution that can match the magnitude of response which you will get with a pharmacological drug, as as stands with with most natural supplements as compared to pharmaceutical formulations. There's a need for increased scientific validation. It's a crowded market, as we've seen. Everybody wants to jump on the bandwagon. There is a place for scientific validation. This is why we are seeing ingredient as well as product companies who want to do trials with us, not just in this area but across the board. We are doing multiple trials because, quite simply, products that have scientific validation increase market resilience, and we've seen that both commercially. Of course, for us, it's great to have the science in the product. As we have seen in the the previous, as we have heard in the previous talk, GLP-1 based products create a need for a secondary demand for supplement products. These may be probiotics, proteins, fiber, multivitamins, due to various reasons. As I said, they may be poor supplementation because there's less absorption, less intake food, or they may be like proteins, which are a true substitute to some extent to the GLP-1 drug. Thank you for your attention.

summary.Summary:
Gulrez Zariwala, founder director of the Centre for Nutraceuticals, asked which supplements aimed at GLP-1 and appetite have science behind them.

He began with the biology. Gut hormones such as GLP-1 and PYY signal fullness, and ghrelin signals hunger. Earlier obesity drugs that acted on the brain carried psychiatric risks, which turned the field to gut hormones. GLP-1 drugs give weight loss of five to 15%, but some of what is lost is muscle.

The boom in GLP-1 supplements, he said, has brought lawsuits, regulatory clampdowns and lower consumer confidence. He then went through the candidates. Proteins have an undisputed effect on GLP-1 release. Berberine, cinnamon and bitter compounds have plausible mechanisms but modest effects and few human studies. His centre's own trials found that potato protein raised GLP-1 as much as whey protein isolate, and that a mulberry extract raised GLP-1 and reduced appetite and food noise.

His conclusion: supplements may fill a gap for current or lapsed users, but none can match a drug, so expectations need managing. Products with scientific validation increase market resilience, and GLP-1 use creates demand for proteins, fibre, probiotics and multivitamins.

Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

This one Otter summary covers the whole recording, which holds two sessions: from-hype-to-proof-the-science (the talk, [00:00] to [25:19]) and beyond-the-glp-1-boom-nutrition (the panel and the host's close, [25:19] to the end).

This meeting explored the intersection of GLP-1 pharmacological trends and the evolving nutraceutical market for weight management and metabolic health.

## Research Insights
**Gorres** presented research from the **Center for Nutraceuticals** regarding endogenous satiety pathways. The discussion focused on how gut hormones like **GLP-1** and **PYY** signal satiety, contrasting them with the hunger-inducing hormone **ghrelin**. 

**Key Research Findings:**
*   **Gorres** highlighted that while **GLP-1** drugs offer significant weight loss (5–15%), they risk muscle mass reduction (sarcopenia) and gastrointestinal side effects.
*   Clinical studies show that dietary proteins, specifically **whey protein isolate** and **potato protein**, can significantly increase post-meal **GLP-1** and **PYY** secretion.
*   A study on **Redicools** (a standardized mulberry extract) demonstrated a reduction in "food noise"—intrusive thoughts regarding food—and appetite.
*   **Berberine** and **cinnamon** were noted for having more modest or indirect effects on weight loss compared to pharmaceutical interventions.

## Market Trends
The panel, including **Nick**, **Brett**, and **Ed**, discussed how the "GLP-1 boom" is turbocharging existing macro trends in the supplement industry.

**Consumer Shifts:**
*   **Nick** observed that consumers starting **GLP-1** treatments often undergo broader behavioral changes, increasing demand for protein, fiber, probiotics, and multivitamins.
*   **Brett** noted that retailers are aggressively expanding the presence of sports nutrition products in mainstream supermarket aisles to capture this demand.
*   There is a rising interest in "beauty from within" products, such as **collagen**, to combat cosmetic side effects like facial fat loss (often termed "**Ozempic face**").
*   **Creatine** is moving into the mainstream as a tier-one ingredient for muscle maintenance among aging populations and weight management users.

## Future Outlook
The discussion concluded with strategic advice for brands navigating this highly regulated and emotional consumer landscape.

**Strategic Considerations:**
*   **Nick** suggested that the greatest unmet need lies in supporting consumers who are "cycling" or coming off **GLP-1** medications to prevent rapid weight regain.
*   **Brett** emphasized the importance of product formulation, specifically creating low-volume, high-nutrient density products (e.g., clear protein with fiber) for users with reduced appetites.
*   **Ed** highlighted the necessity of nutritional education for athletes to prevent micronutrient deficiencies during periods of suppressed caloric intake.
*   How can brands effectively use AI to provide personalized education while maintaining strict regulatory compliance?

- Speaker 3 - : Develop a protein-plus-fiber product and expand the fiber range with a more complex fiber blend.
- Speaker 5 - : Organize and hold next year's two-day conference at Novotel London West from December 7 through 10.

- Speaker 1 - : Continue the RediCools study long term and evaluate effects on body weight and body composition, subject to industry-partner support.

summary.Summary:
The day's last panel asked what GLP-1 means for sports and active nutrition beyond the boom. It brought together Nick Morgan of Nutrition Integrated, Brett Hamer, product director at Myprotein, and Ed Tooley, a performance nutritionist.

They agreed that GLP-1 is speeding up trends that already existed rather than creating new ones, and that few brands put GLP-1 on pack: Myprotein sells need-state bundles, and retailer bays such as Boots' let brands be present without the wording. Brett said clear protein, and clear protein with collagen, is selling very well to this consumer, while plant protein has not taken off; Nick put that down to taste. Nick called creatine almost a tier one ingredient, now bought by women, older consumers and people managing their weight.

They differed in where they looked. Ed's concern was nutrition: people who simply eat less risk missing protein, carbohydrate and micronutrients, so he puts protein first. Brett and Nick looked at products: both would launch protein with fibre, and Nick named low-volume clear protein with fibre and products for people coming off the drugs as the gaps. For the next disruptor, Brett named people coming off the drugs, Ed education between on and off, and Nick AI.

The recording ends with the host's close of the day.

This one Otter summary covers the whole recording, which holds two sessions: from-hype-to-proof-the-science (the talk, [00:00] to [25:19]) and beyond-the-glp-1-boom-nutrition (the panel and the host's close, [25:19] to the end).

This meeting explored the intersection of GLP-1 pharmacological trends and the evolving nutraceutical market for weight management and metabolic health.

## Research Insights
**Gorres** presented research from the **Center for Nutraceuticals** regarding endogenous satiety pathways. The discussion focused on how gut hormones like **GLP-1** and **PYY** signal satiety, contrasting them with the hunger-inducing hormone **ghrelin**. 

**Key Research Findings:**
*   **Gorres** highlighted that while **GLP-1** drugs offer significant weight loss (5–15%), they risk muscle mass reduction (sarcopenia) and gastrointestinal side effects.
*   Clinical studies show that dietary proteins, specifically **whey protein isolate** and **potato protein**, can significantly increase post-meal **GLP-1** and **PYY** secretion.
*   A study on **Redicools** (a standardized mulberry extract) demonstrated a reduction in "food noise"—intrusive thoughts regarding food—and appetite.
*   **Berberine** and **cinnamon** were noted for having more modest or indirect effects on weight loss compared to pharmaceutical interventions.

## Market Trends
The panel, including **Nick**, **Brett**, and **Ed**, discussed how the "GLP-1 boom" is turbocharging existing macro trends in the supplement industry.

**Consumer Shifts:**
*   **Nick** observed that consumers starting **GLP-1** treatments often undergo broader behavioral changes, increasing demand for protein, fiber, probiotics, and multivitamins.
*   **Brett** noted that retailers are aggressively expanding the presence of sports nutrition products in mainstream supermarket aisles to capture this demand.
*   There is a rising interest in "beauty from within" products, such as **collagen**, to combat cosmetic side effects like facial fat loss (often termed "**Ozempic face**").
*   **Creatine** is moving into the mainstream as a tier-one ingredient for muscle maintenance among aging populations and weight management users.

## Future Outlook
The discussion concluded with strategic advice for brands navigating this highly regulated and emotional consumer landscape.

**Strategic Considerations:**
*   **Nick** suggested that the greatest unmet need lies in supporting consumers who are "cycling" or coming off **GLP-1** medications to prevent rapid weight regain.
*   **Brett** emphasized the importance of product formulation, specifically creating low-volume, high-nutrient density products (e.g., clear protein with fiber) for users with reduced appetites.
*   **Ed** highlighted the necessity of nutritional education for athletes to prevent micronutrient deficiencies during periods of suppressed caloric intake.
*   How can brands effectively use AI to provide personalized education while maintaining strict regulatory compliance?

# Nick Morgan: how longevity is sold, from hallmarks to habits: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Nick Morgan - Remedy CDMO", https://otter.ai/u/e7RrbCs2RWPnhgDD_ew_dnFqZNc, recorded 22 Oct 2026 11:50, 6m 13s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Speaker 1: And you've got a lot of longevity sitting in women's health because the two tend to go together. Beauty in itself, people think about that in the context of aging and wrinkles and so on. Menopause is a distinct life phase, and also now people increasingly see sports nutrition as a category as a conduit to living better. So people are developing products with a specific focus here. They're developing products with a specific focus here and here, and they're actually quite different. And you'll see brands do it differently. Now, interestingly, if you take about 300 products and you code how they communicate, I think it's really interesting because loads of people still use longevity, even though it's the numerical value to which you will live. But interesting, if you come down here, more people talk about energy and vitality. That's their consumer connection. And if you look further down, the hallmarks are hardly explained. 9% will refer to the hallmarks. Only 4% I think, will actually place them in any lead copy. So actually, the hallmarks of aging is for this people in this room. Most consumers couldn't get two hoots, except for the very small few. So it's really interesting when you start to get that. But cellular health becomes the focus area that appears everywhere. That's between. That's almost become a surrogate for longevity and healthy aging is a target concern, and that's where you start to see all of this come through. Very few people will talk about the entirety of all hallmarks of aging. Now, in terms of how people communicate, how do people bring this to life in products? Now, first and foremost, if you just want to know some of the top ingredients people use, then if I took another 300 products that placed themselves on the longevity shelf, you will see recognizable ingredients like resveratrol, coq10, ubiquinol fit underneath that, spermidine, and so on. But what's really interesting is you don't sell one product in 2026. That would be a crazy thing to do. What you need to do is resonate with a consumer about that they want support ritualistically and through the lens of habits. They want you to say, "I'm going to support your longevity. It's not one magic product. It's probably three. Now, Solero is just one example of actually a brand that sells you a core routine and a habit. They have an A, a B, and a C. I'll let you look at those in your own time. But they're an AM, a PM, and I love the third. If anyone knows it, it's a product you take for two days every month. That's it. Just two days in the month done. It's the reset. A little bit different. But what I thought was interesting was they talk about interconnected. They do talk about the hallmarks of aging, and what do they use? Three products, one simple routine. In today's world, you might sell an ingredient, but what you're selling to your customers is how you fit into their product systems: an A, B, C, a 123, an A, M, it's not a one-dimensional approach to product; it's a multifaceted approach to how you help people adapt their habits and rituals aligned to their goals. Now, in terms of moving on, what we also find that it's a bloody expensive category. So, if you want to go and buy some products, then actually they are really expensive. Now, I'll just point out here: this is the price per serve, normalized in euros across a number of categories. Here is some longevity, and they're expensive. And actually, they'll be some of the most expensive products you'll find in the industry. Now, I just want to point you to this little number here. The average for creatine median per serve is around about 50 cents, right? It's maybe a little bit lower, but you can take an existing ingredient, call it longevity, and actually be a hell of a lot more expensive. So I'm taking this ingredient, putting longevity on the front of it, and you can make it really expensive. So even your existing ingredients, if they are relevant, you can turn into a premium proposition just by the beauty of telling a great story. By the way, I 100% buy into the role of creatine anyway. It's a daily essential for me, so it's not an example for anything other than I think it's a great way of trying to dissociate from a traditional category and making it relevant for people who are buying this need. Now, just to finish off with 35 seconds to go, longevity 2.0-it's already moving fast. I just want to point out that there are three things that I think are happening. It's not just capsules, although 70% of all the products we see are in capsule format. So, for those who make capsules, that will be music-terriers. But we are seeing massive changes in format and accessibility. You can actually buy a sperm and iron pen. It's a cartridge. You inject it. Interestingly, almost going back to being a little bit more precision. But we are seeing liquids, of course. We're seeing chocolates. Who doesn't love the emotion of a chocolate to make you feel better? If I can make that chocolate have a little bit of longevity to it, then wow, what a double whammy! So that's a beautiful interaction. But what's the point? They're becoming more accessible in more products, more gummies, more liquids, more drinks. There's an energy drink with NAD in it in today's world, and that's where we are. We are also seeing cellular health and cellular claims come into very big categories like hydration, the description of cellular hydration, cellular health in there, and we're also seeing a massive shift to sports nutrition. And this is Sergio Ramos. For those of you that know your footballers, he's linked to a brand called Centenarian, beautiful name, and that is all about real longevity, backed by science, delivered through sports nutrition. It is moving fast. Get on that train and challenge yourself to stay on top of it. Because what you communicate today will be different in a few weeks or months. That's what I told you. Remember those five things, and good luck. luck. Thank you very much indeed. I do like the idea of vlog gathering chocolate. That sort of appeals. Although

summary.Summary:
The recording catches the last six minutes of Nick Morgan's talk on the longevity consumer. His question was how brands actually sell longevity, and his answer was: not through the science.

Longevity now sits inside women's health, menopause and sports nutrition. Consumers connect with "energy and vitality" and "cellular health", not the hallmarks of ageing; in about 300 products he coded, only 9% refer to the hallmarks at all. Brands sell a routine of about three products, not one, so an ingredient is sold on how it fits the customer's product system.

Longevity is also one of the most expensive categories per serve. His example was creatine: a median of about 50 cents a serve on the sports shelf, and far more with longevity on the front of the pack. A good story can turn an existing ingredient into a premium one.

He closed on where the category is going. Capsules dominate today, but formats are widening into liquids, chocolate, gummies and drinks, cellular claims are entering hydration, and longevity is moving into sports nutrition. His advice was to keep up, because what brands say today will change within months.

Nick Morgan discusses the evolving consumer landscape, communication strategies, and product formats within the longevity and healthy aging market.

## Market Communication
**Nick** notes that while "longevity" is a technical term, consumers connect more with concepts like "energy," "vitality," and "cellular health." Most brands avoid technical "hallmarks of aging" in lead copy, as only 4% to 9% of products utilize them effectively for a general audience.
**Consumer Trends**
*   Longevity is increasingly linked to women's health (menopause) and sports nutrition.
*   "Cellular health" has become a widely used surrogate for longevity.

## Product Strategy
**Nick** emphasizes that success in 2026 requires selling routines rather than single products. Brands should focus on multifaceted approaches that integrate into daily habits and rituals.
**Pricing and Ingredients**
*   Common ingredients include **resveratrol**, **CoQ10**, **ubiquinol**, and **spermidine**.
*   Longevity products command premium pricing; for example, even traditional ingredients like **creatine** can be repositioned as high-end longevity products through better storytelling.
*   The brand **Solero** is cited as an example of a successful routine-based model using AM, PM, and monthly "reset" products.

## Future Formats
The longevity category is moving beyond the standard capsule format, which currently accounts for 70% of the market. New delivery methods are increasing accessibility and consumer engagement.
**Emerging Delivery Methods**
*   Liquids, gummies, chocolates, and energy drinks (e.g., drinks containing **NAD**).
*   Precision delivery methods such as injection pens/cartridges.
*   Integration into broader categories like hydration and sports nutrition, exemplified by the brand **Centenarian**.

## Discovery Technology
**Miguel** introduced **Nuritas** as an R&D-focused company based in Dublin that utilizes a proprietary artificial intelligence platform to identify new peptide molecules. The process involves defining a mechanism of action or consumer need and using the **AI** to narrow down candidates for subsequent *in vitro* and *in vivo* testing. This method aims to reduce the discovery timeline to approximately two years while increasing cost-efficiency and accuracy. **Miguel** also noted that the company maintains a library of over 9 million peptides, including a new non-hormonal peptide for sleep.

**Brian** detailed the functionality of **PeptiStrong**, a protein hydrolysate derived from fava bean, which acts by activating or inhibiting specific biological pathways.

**Miguel** addressed regulatory considerations regarding EFSA claims and mentioned that they work with partners like **Vivatis** to define labelable benefits for customers. He highlighted recent expansion into Poland and emphasized their openness to new partnerships through the **Remedy CDMO** platform, noting a current development project with **Tantus**.

## Product Overview
**Ubiquinol** is the active, reduced form of **Coenzyme Q10**, which provides direct benefits to the body without requiring conversion by the enzyme diaphorase—an enzyme that decreases with age.

**Kaneka** produces **Ubiquinol** in Japan and maintains high quality standards through extensive research and various certifications.
* **Formulations**: Available in pure form for soft capsules, gel pills, or gummies, and in a microencapsulated form for diverse dosage formats.
* **Quality assurance**: Supported by over 100 clinical studies, **Halal** certification, and multiple innovation awards.
* **Logistics**: **Kaneka** serves the European market via a warehouse in Belgium to ensure short lead times.

# Martin Bauer: Rhosera, cultivated Rhodiola rosea against anabolic resistance: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Rhosera - Martin Bauer - Remedy CDMO", https://otter.ai/u/h-He1KRLsyjlt0MtiA_KezhS81k, recorded 22 Oct 2026 13:07, 16m 16s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Speaker 1: I realize that I'm the last one before lunch, so I try to give my best to keep you awake until we finally can go to the deserved break. So my name is Ralph. I'm coming from the Martin Bauer Nutritions Company and have the pleasure to introduce our latest ingredient, which is called Rosera. And I would like to tell you in the next 50 minutes, what's it's all about longevity and what does it mean beyond protein? Before I go there, okay, I would like to lose a couple of words about the company I'm representing. So I'm coming from Nathan Bawa Nutraceuticals. The Nathan Bawa Nutraceutical is a newly formed organization within the Nature Network. The Nature Network is a privately owned holding in a fourth generation, and I think we do have a lot of companies dedicated all around botanicals. The biggest one is Martin Bauer itself, was set up in 1930, and they are the vanguard for botanicals, meaning they are doing all the cultivation, all the sourcing of the herbs we are using, they are very big in the tea industry. Also, if you want to look for RTD drinks in the beverage industry, they are also very big in that. Then we do have Finselberg, where I am originally from. That is the oldest unit in our company. That's from 1875. They do extracts for the pharmaceutical, and depending on the legislation, also on the supplement industry, and last but not least, we have a very big third-party lab that's called PhyterLab. They do all type analysis around herbals, not only regular analysis, also reference substance, and also the growing mountains of contaminants. Yeah, the company has 4,300 people worldwide. We have a lot of, let's say, manufacturing sites. I think over 30 here in Poland. We are represented by Martin Bovatska and Vita Chiche. We do have, I think, in Klenkari Phyto Farm, in the Europlant Group, in Posnan. Maybe one or the other had already contact with them. Okay, what was the motivation for us to develop Rosera? And I mean, Rosera is, as the name maybe sounds familiar, is based on a plant called Rudiolar Rosera. It's nothing new on the horizon. However, you will see that there are some secrets in that plant based on the cultivated material, and the motivation for us was really the aging population. If you look at the numbers here, I mean it's not a secret, but 2050 we will have probably over 2 billion people 60 years and older, and we have identified a gap in the health industry, and this is a gap of the aging of a muscle cell, I mean, when you are 25 or 30, you start already aging, and you will lose muscle, unnoticeable basically. But when you are 60, it becomes a real problem. We addressed it a couple of times. You will lose muscle exponentially, especially if you get hospital. I try to speak loud because the organ allows to speak loud, and I think not to lose time. I would like to address one problem, which is quite important as the when you're aging. I mean, people try to overcome their problem. While eating more protein, I mean, usually the recommendation is 0.8 gram protein. When you have normal age, when you're aging, you are 1.2 gram. But why you need more protein? It's the reason is because your muscle cell cannot longer efficiently utilize protein while you are aging. I mean, this process is known as anabolic resistance, and there is hardly any ingredient on the market which is really trying to fill this gap by enabling a muscle cell to utilize protein more efficiently, and that was our motivation. And I think the biggest problem right now is when you talk about Ruliola rosea, it's a very famous adaptogen. I mean, it's on the market here since 30 years. I mean, has a history a long time ago, but really as a supplement, it has become popular last 30 years as an adaptogen, and it became so popular that it was overharvested because usually it was connected widely in Mother Nature. It's a root, and once the root is out of the soil, that's the problem. The plant is gone. And I mean, if you want to build up or create a brand based on rhodiola rosea, you have to be aware of the risks. I mean, there's currently already a risk of the supply chain. When something becomes scary, I mean, you also need to be aware that, especially in the botanical area, you have a lot of creative guys. I mean, adulterating the market with different species or with different creations, and of course, you have a lot of regulatory and reputational hurdles to overcome. And by 2023, rhodiola was put on the scientist list as an endangered species. And since we were dealing with rhodiola since 30 years, we asked ourselves a very simple question: What if we do cultivate rhodiola on our own? So we did, and I think nowadays we have over 25 years' experience in cultivation of rhodiola under our rhodiola platform. What we are doing, we have three selected mother lines where we get our seeds from. We then just breed our seedlings. You can see here on the left-hand side. These seedlings will be then raised to a certain size. Then we will be transplanted into the soil. We give it to the farmer, and the farmer not just sits there and waits until it grows three or four years. Now it is what we are calling a controlled, integrated cultivation. That means the farmer is not allowed to use it. Pesticides, or he cannot just. He needs to make a manual weed control in order to avoid that pyrazidic alkaline weeds are contaminating the problem, the product, because one plant can already contaminate a complete hectare, and I think that is something which we have really built within a couple of years. I mean that was not easy. If you think you can just go into the wild, pick some seeds, put it into soil, and wait and see, and you have a cultivation. Unfortunately, it doesn't work. If you look at here at our cultivation history, it took us over 10 years to get from over 240 different accessions from rhodiola. Finally, three elite lines, and these three elite lines were really lines we are using today after 10 years of development, for expanding our rhodiola cultivation. So, what does the cultivation gives us? First of all, it gives us a completely different fingerprint, but luckily not qualitatively, but quantitatively. What you see that's quite typical for cultivated plant is they are in a cozy environment. They don't need to, I mean, fight against the cold. They don't need to fight against food limitations and stuff like that, and UV light. So they usually have lower metabolites compared to the higher metabolites you have in plants. You see usually outside in the wilderness, and when you see at the fingerprints there, they are more or less identically identical qualitatively, but quantitatively you see a lot of precursors dominating. And I think this you can see already here on the next slide, where we were able to identify a lot of processes which will be initiated only by the cultivated material. First of all, you see that there's an upregulation of certain genes. One gene is Pax7, the other one is myod. I mean, Pak7 is basically waking up dormant stem cells, and the myod is basically giving them a blueprint to tell them how to grow and how to differentiate. And what you can also see is that some of these pathways will be triggered as well. And some of these pathways are very important, like the folic acid pathways for DNA generation, or for instance the polyamine pathways. Polyamine we talked about one of the most famous, prominent polyamines today already. Spermidim, speramine, putrycene. I mean, they will be all generated in Z2 where they belong, and you don't have to take them externally and then ask and pray that they finally get to their goal. And I think you can see that this is just a very big difference which we have seen, and I mean it does not happen in the wildcrafted material at all. However, as I told before, it's just a matter of concentration because the wildcrafted material also contains. These substances, but in a much lower concentration. So, if you concentrate a wildcrafted material by a factor of 2.5, you will see similar effects starting on a cell level. Of course, that all happened here in a cell, and of course, I mean, a cell is not a real human body. You don't have a bad night in a cell. You don't have whatever bad absorption or stress, so you need to confirm it in a real-world environment. So we just did it in a clinical trial, and what we did was quite our standard. These people had a slight loss on muscle, no sarcopenia. I mean, they were still considered healthy, but untrained, and we divided them in two groups, and both groups received the defined amount of training. So without training, just sitting on your sofa, no muscle will go. The hand grip test is one of the most important biomarkers for longevity. I mean, if you just fall short on that hand grip test, I mean, your longevity is also not so long anymore. He called them the best results he had seen with a botanical in 31 years.

Ralph introduces **Rhosera**, a cultivated **Rhodiola rosea** ingredient designed to combat anabolic resistance and muscle aging.

## Product Overview
**Ralph** presents **Rhosera**, a botanical ingredient derived from a proprietary cultivation of **Rhodiola rosea**. The product aims to address the health gap caused by an aging population, specifically targeting "anabolic resistance," where aging muscle cells become less efficient at utilizing protein. 

**Cultivation and Quality**
*   **Martin Bauer** utilizes a controlled, integrated cultivation process developed over 10 years to identify three elite mother lines.
*   Unlike wild-harvested plants, which are endangered and prone to adulteration, this cultivated material is grown in Central Europe without pesticides.
*   The cultivated material shows significantly higher concentrations (4 to 5-fold) of key metabolites like **rhodiolene**, **glycosyl**, and **rhodiocyanide A** compared to wild variants.
*   Preclinical data indicates the ingredient upregulates specific genes, including **Pax7** (to activate stem cells) and **myod** (for differentiation), while triggering polyamine pathways.

## Clinical Results
**Ralph** shared findings from a double-blind, placebo-controlled study involving 140 untrained adults aged 55 to 75. Participants received a daily dose of 400mg of **Rhosera** alongside defined training and protein intake.

**Key Outcomes**
*   **Muscle Soreness:** Delayed onset of muscle soreness was reduced by 46% in men and 52% in women.
*   **Physical Performance:** Statistically significant improvements were recorded in chair stand tests, single leg balance, bench press, and leg press.
*   **Longevity Biomarkers:** Improvements were noted in hand grip strength, a critical biomarker for longevity.
*   **Mental Well-being:** Participants reported reduced fatigue, improved quality of life, and increased motivation/social engagement.

## Formulation Guidance
For manufacturers looking to incorporate **Rhosera**, **Ralph** provided several technical recommendations and compliance notes.

**Usage Details**
*   Recommended dosage: 250mg to 350mg per formula.
*   Compatible formats: Tablets, capsules, bars, and V caps.
*   Beverage application: While possible, it is challenging due to the inherent bitterness of **Rhodiola**.
*   Regulatory status: The product is 100% plant-based and sustainable; however, since direct **EFSA** claims for **Rhodiola** are limited, formulators may need to use permitted auxiliary claims related to magnesium or vitamin B to address fatigue.

Thomas presented Solabia Nutrition's approach to successful product launches by addressing the practical limitations of standard industry briefs.

## Marketing Strategy
**Thomas** emphasized that a product must be memorable to succeed in the market. He shared two case studies regarding rebranding:
* **Microbiomex**, a flavonol with prebiotic effects, was rebranded as **Copilot Freedom Probiotic** because "flavorbiotic" was too difficult for consumers to understand and remember.
* **Aronia berry extract**, clinically studied for cognitive benefits, was renamed **Brainberry**, which has become the second largest and fastest-growing product in their portfolio.

## Manufacturing Challenges
Successful products require balancing complex ingredient lists with physical stability and delivery formats. 
* Creating products with high doses of multiple ingredients (e.g., 3–5g of creatine or 5–10g of collagen) can lead to issues with solubility and stomach mixing.
* **Thomas** highlighted a partnership with the CDMO **Tantus** to solve creatine degradation in gummies caused by heat application. By using a cold-pressed tablet method combined with **WhatsApp** (a citrus extract), they maintain the integrity of the creatine while supporting nitric oxide production and blood flow.

## Scientific Validity
To avoid meaningless "science-backed" claims, **Thomas** argued that brands must focus on transparent, rigorous data including dose, population, and placebo-controlled endpoints. 
* **Solabia Nutrition** provides open-source access to their study summaries via their website. 
* An example provided was **Bun Olive**, an olive leaf extract used for skin health and menopause symptoms; all relevant studies were conducted on women by female-led research teams to ensure demographic accuracy.

Tantus presents its strategic approach to transforming longevity trends into consumer-ready products through simplified formulations and strategic partnerships.

## Product Strategy
**Victoria** and **Mateus** discussed the shift in consumer focus from lifespan to healthspan, emphasizing the need for products that support active and independent living. The company's core philosophy centers on simplicity and ease of use to ensure long-term consumer compliance.

**Development Process**
The team follows a four-step methodology to move from concept to market:
1. Trend analysis involving market development and scientific research.
2. Ingredient selection based on scientific rationale rather than marketing alone.
3. Formulation focusing on dosage, delivery form, and compatibility.
4. Market implementation through manufacturing and concept demonstration.

## Strategic Partnerships
**Mateus** highlighted that **Tantus** views suppliers as partners rather than mere vendors to gain access to deep technical knowledge, scientific research, and formulation expertise. This collaborative approach allows for co-creating product concepts rather than just purchasing raw materials.

## Product Concepts

# The Protein Brewery: Fermotein, a fermented mycelium protein for active and all-in-one nutrition: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Thijs - Fermotein - Remedy CDMO", https://otter.ai/u/ZXyx5ZOSuM5zfKku6YMQxaU1pFA, recorded 22 Oct 2026 15:33, 8m 25s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Speaker 1: Thank you. Let's see. Yeah, my name is Tais Bos. I'm the CEO of the Protein Brewery. I actually have quite a long background in selling and developing protein ingredients. So I was at Fonterra, where I headed up their European whey business, and then at at Cosun selling fava proteins. But now I'm really in a space which I really like, which is selling more complex and more sustainable ingredients. So, yeah, our company is the Protein Brewery. We are a brewery of of proteins, so we are a biomass fermentation company. We grow mycelium in bioreactors and we turn that in a super exciting ingredient. I'm going to tell you a little bit about our company. We're probably one of the youngest companies here, so we exist now for six years. Founded in 2020 from the lab into the pilot plant into a commercial scale facility, what we have now in Breda, in the Netherlands, two 85,000 liter fermenters and expanding rapidly. And we are the first mycelium protein company that has EFSA approval. So since the summer of this year, we can finally sell in Europe, but over the last couple of years, we have developed mainly the market in the U.S. which is why I'm going to give you a few examples of the U.S. market. I hope this works. So this is a little video. Let's see. It should start like this. It's made by one of our operators. It's a bit of an artist impression. So this is our factory of our manufacturing process. You see a lot of oxygen, and you see the mycelium growing in the in the bioreactor. What we make is what we grow is a fungal strain, so it comes from fungi. So we brew that in the bioreactor. It forms these hy-Vee, and it consists of protein, prebiotic fiber, and bioactives. And then ultimately, we take the liquid out of the bioreactor and we turn it into a powder through downstream processing. And that powder is then applied in shakes and applications, like you see here. So it's one of our process operators putting AI video making to the to practice, which is really cool to see. So you heard, I think Nick talking about spermidine around longevity. I think a couple of others, including Tentis, were talking about muscle health. Yeah, we have protein in our ingredient, 50% complete protein, 30% prebiotic fiber. It's mainly chitin and chitosan, which is very specific to our type of fungi. Then it's very rich in spermidine, seven times higher than, for example, in beet germ. So it's about 1700 milligrams per kilo, and then very rich in different types of vitamins, especially choline, precursor for b4. So we have all of these different components into one one ingredient, which we mainly use into active nutrition applications. So yeah, I think this is why I really like selling this ingredient. So it's very new, very novel, but I don't think anything else is is out there on the market that combines combines these type of ingredients into one. As I mentioned, so we have been commercializing this in the U.S. because it took a while, took five years to get approved by FSA in Europe, which we now finally have, but now yeah, we we sell into the U.S. and it's mainly into the all-in-one nutrition segment, which hasn't really evolved yet. I think in in Europe you have the wholemeal replacers like U-well and Wyfoot, but in in the U.S. you have brands like Cajava that have developed a category of their own, and it's basically yeah all the nutrition you need from one one type of powder. It's still small, but it's growing really fast. And everybody knows, of course, the protein powder segment, and then also the the meal replacement segment. And it's literally sitting sitting in between. Yeah, one one example is indeed Iskachava. They're one of the fastest growing brands listed in in retail like Walmart, but also selling a lot through the online stores, and they position themselves really as a protein and fiber combination, which you can use in your everyday ritual. So you, for example, use it in a breakfast smoothie or or over lunch. They like it's still still a small company, but they are super profitable, and actually you can see like different types of formats that they use, like all the way from like two-pound bags, like your standard 1 kg bag of protein powder, to larger tubs, but also single serve bags. And obviously, the price increase increases by the small base that you sell sell into the format. Yeah, a couple of couple of other examples. So, for example, one superfood. I think a lot of you, all of you, will probably know AG1, so like the superfood powders. In the US, now new formats and categories are emerging, also catering into all-in-one nutrition. So you have the superfood, and you combine it with protein and fiber. Obviously, for ingredients such as ours, it's a really good fit because we can add promoting our ingredient to to the superfood category, and then yeah, what we've seen in Europe is like I think it it will come, and and hopefully a couple of CMOs or CDMOs here will will embrace the concept. Meal replacement, so like a meal in a bottle or into a into a powder into a bar has been around for quite a long time. So you all recently sold to Danone, Why Food sold to Nestle. So the big FMCG companies are definitely looking into this. But it's still like a meal replacement concept and not an all-in-one nutrition concept. Then a little bit about promoting in our science. So we see ourselves. Although we're a young company, we invest quite heavily in preclinical and clinical science. So we've done studies on the prebiotic effects of our ingredients, so mainly short-chain fatty acids, microbial and alpha diversity in the gut. Given that our fibers are very different from other fibers that are around in the diet, it has a very positive effect. It has a positive effect on GLP-1, and we did a very interesting study with Nema Live on C. elegans, so the nematodes, where fermentin is proven to increase lifespan in the nematodes by 22% We're doing now a follow-up study on that to get to see what actually causes that that specific result, and we're also going to do a human clinical study on that. So click through this quite quickly on the biological aging clock. So we're doing that together with the University of Wageningen in quarter one, large-scale human clinical trial to yeah to measure that. Yeah, that's it. There it is. Together with with Paul Gössfaifers. Yeah. Then at the moment, so we're we're scaling up our company. We're heavily investing in extra production capacity because being a startup, like we have to, and that's partly my job as a CEO as well. We have to raise money because we're definitely not yet profitable. We're scaling up scaling up the production in our factory in Breidan, and then we're also like commercializing the ingredient in in the U.S. and in Europe. So at the moment we have 10 million servings sold in 2026. Three customers now in the U.S. that have launched with with the ingredient, mainly in the active nutrition space, but also in all-in-one nutrition. A lot of prospects in the European pipeline. So like if you want to try the product, I have it at our table in in the hallway. We have a neutral flavored one and an iced coffee flavor. We've raised quite a bit of money up until now. So, over the last six years, we did three investment rounds. So, we raised 70 million. Nova Holdings, so the the parent company of Nova Nessus and Nova Nordisk is our biggest shareholder, and as I mentioned, we're now now approved by EFSA. We're also approved in Singapore, and we're going after approval in in Australia and in Canada. Then let's see, yeah, where I took this opportunity where we're nominated for one of the top companies to watch by Protein Technology magazine. So if you want to vote for us, that's much appreciated. And if you want to connect with us through LinkedIn, yeah, let us know. And yeah, happy to meet a lot of you and answer your questions in in the breaks in today and tomorrow. Thank you. Thank you very much indeed, Tice.

summary.Summary:
Thijs Bos, CEO of The Protein Brewery and formerly a seller of dairy and fava proteins, presented Fermotein, a mycelium ingredient grown by biomass fermentation in Breda, in the Netherlands. His pitch was that one ingredient can carry protein, fibre and longevity bioactives together.

He said Fermotein is 50% complete protein and 30% prebiotic fibre, and is rich in spermidine and choline. It is the first mycelium protein with EFSA approval, which came this summer after five years. While waiting, the company built its market in the US, in "all-in-one nutrition": powders that sit between protein powder and meal replacement, with Ka'Chava as the model. Superfood powders are adding protein and fibre too. In Europe meal replacement is still the nearest category, and he asked the CDMOs in the room to embrace the all-in-one concept.

On evidence he cited prebiotic studies, a positive effect on GLP-1, and a nematode study in which Fermotein extended lifespan, with a human trial on a biological ageing clock planned with Wageningen University.

He closed on scale: 10 million servings sold in 2026, three US customers launched, and 70 million raised, with Novo Holdings the largest shareholder. The company is not yet profitable.

**Thijs** presents **The Protein Brewery**, a biomass fermentation company specializing in mycelium-based protein ingredients.

## Company Overview
**Thijs** describes **The Protein Brewery** as a six-year-old company founded in 2020 that utilizes bioreactors to grow fungal strains.
*   **Production Infrastructure**: The facility in Breda, Netherlands, currently operates two 85,000-liter fermenters with plans for rapid expansion.
*   **Regulatory Status**: The company has secured **EFSA** approval for sale in Europe as of summer 2024, alongside approval in Singapore. Applications are pending in Australia and Canada.
*   **Financials**: The company has raised 70 million through three investment rounds, with **Novo Holdings** (parent of **Novo Nordisk**) as the largest shareholder.

## Product Details
The core product is a mycelium-based powder derived from fungal hyphae via downstream processing.
*   **Nutritional Profile**: The ingredient consists of 50% complete protein, 30% prebiotic fiber (primarily chitin and chitosan), and is rich in spermidine (1700 mg/kg, seven times higher than wheat germ), vitamins, and choline.
*   **Market Strategy**: While primarily targeting the U.S. "all-in-one nutrition" segment—citing brands like **Ka'Chava** as successful examples—the company is now expanding into Europe following **EFSA** clearance.
*   **Commercial Traction**: As of 2026 projections, the company aims for 10 million servings sold, currently maintaining three customers in the U.S. active nutrition space and a growing European pipeline.

## Scientific Research
**Thijs** emphasizes heavy investment in preclinical and clinical studies to validate the ingredient's health benefits.
*   **Gut Health**: Studies have focused on prebiotic effects, specifically short-chain fatty acids, microbial diversity, and positive effects on GLP-1.
*   **Longevity**: Research using *C. elegans* showed that **Fermotein** increased lifespan by 22%.
*   **Future Studies**: A large-scale human clinical trial regarding biological aging clocks is scheduled for Q1 in collaboration with the **University of Wageningen**.
