sessions.transcript:
# Holland & Barrett: how longevity science translates into consumer outcomes: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Alex Glover - H&B - Remedy CDMO", https://otter.ai/u/LXa2bHODxRY5s8up7grRiBmKTgI, recorded 22 Oct 2026 15:50, 10m 43s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Speaker 1: Factoring and all the decisions that go with it, and then finally the customer's first question is: Is it on offer? Our next session considers how long Gavity Science translates into the relevant consumer outcomes. From strategic partner Holland and Barrett, please welcome Alex Glover. Probably best use one of those that's up there, I think.
[00:25] Speaker 2: Thank you. Yes, great. Everybody can hear me. So, hello, everyone. My name is Alex. So, I lead the product formulation team at Holden Barrack Global. I'm responsible for all of the own label products that Holden Barrett formulate and develop across the globe. And I'm really happy that you started out there saying is we are with you saying about deciding what to buy because that's really the information that we get as a retailer all the time, is why a customer is choosing to buy our products and it's how we communicate that the border of being scientifically led, a clinical outcome, and combining it with a customer outcome because customers don't speak clinical language, so that's the agenda, which we will skip over. So, there's a photograph of a tortoise on the screen, and I really like this this analogy because it was one of the first lectures I ever had doing my master's program. Was this exact image put up on the screen? So, why is there a tortoise on the screen? This is why there's a tortoise on the screen? A tortoise's biology fundamentally challenges the way we look at aging. A tortoise will live the majority of its life without any disability or ailment. As you compare to a human, we live approximately between 10 and 12 years with either a disability or poor health. So a tortoise fundamentally will challenge the notion that biology is we are destined to age in a poor way. I'm not saying we're all going to live to 200 years, but actually there is a biological plausibility that we can all age better. So it's not just smoke and mirrors. Lifespan to health. Nick touched on this very nicely in his talk about the difference between the two, and it's a really important distinction because I think the category should almost be renamed, not just longevity, because actually, we're not in the business of making people live longer; we're making them live better. How do we do that from a product perspective? So, we're in a very, very fortunate position where we have data of millions of consumers across the globe, and we can see what they're buying and how frequently they're buying it, which is obviously the most important thing that we all, as brand owners, want. Is we want customers not just to buy the product once, we want them to keep buying the product. So, I see a lot of this in the kind of cellular health space and the more novels products in the in the longevity spaces. They promise a lot from mechanism. It's all about sirtuins and parts and telomere lengths, and I think I was on a really interesting panel last week in London with our with our own customers. So we were talking to all of our customers. We had customers from all of our key groups, and we had customers from each of our key markets. And something that really stood out to me was the way that customers talk to us about our products. So we think we can communicate to the customer with the science and the claims, but the way customers talk to us. For example, there was there was a lady in one of our customer groups called Stay Healthies. These are customers around the 50 age group, and she was just saying, "Well, actually, all I want to be able to do is play with my grandchildren, get up out of my chair without making a noise, go on that hike, travel without being uncomfortable, and this is not something that we've seen in clinical literature about how can how can I play with my grandchildren, but actually it's how we translate scientific evidence to help consumers with their problems, and not just looking at what the science is saying. And this really does retain customers. So we see the biggest sales that in our own label portfolio is products that have a clear communicated benefit to joint function, joint comfort, brain function, etc. These things like this, not just focusing on disseminating the clinical literature. So yeah, they do not buy. So this is a really interesting point, and I had a bit of a debate with our science team about this one last week. Customers are not buying into the mechanism. They are buying your product based off how they feel and how they continue to feel taking your product. So, common questions that we get as a retailer all the time is when timescale. When am I going to feel a benefit? What kind of benefit am I going to feel taking the product? And that's when we look to lean on the science because we can say, well, the population we saw a benefit within four weeks, within eight weeks, within six weeks, and with a strong scientific communication strategy that we have as a brand, we can sometimes communicate those things to the customer on pack. Can I measure it? Do I feel an improvement? Can I walk without pain? Can I play longer with my grandchild? Can I walk a little bit longer? Can I travel in more comfort? These are some of the really common ones that we get. And how much is it going to cost? I think Nick's slide said it really well. I think was it one euro 36 or something? And actually, some of the most cost effective evidence based interventions to improve longevity are nutritional interventions. Things like fiber, vitamin D, calcium, protein. All of these things have a really high level of evidence compared to some other newer, more novel technologies, and they're really cost-effective. Vitamin D, I think, costs about two cents per 10 microgram serving. I worked out from our from our own label. Most of our customers are not asking or saying, "What's my NAD level? How long are my telomeres? Are my siruin scavenging free radicals, or how active are my parts? I have never once heard any of those things from our customers. It's not to say they don't matter. The evidence gap. So when I'm talking to ingredient ingredient suppliers all the time, and I'm very immersed in clinical research, and a lot of the time, I'm seeing ingredients and the industry getting stuck in the first two blue sections of this. We're very focused on mechanism. We're very focused on biomarkers, but we're not focused on not just the clinical outcome, the customer outcome. What does the customer want? So, for example, if we take sleep, you know, I had a an ingredient the other day I was reading about, and they were constantly talking about the Pittsburgh Sleep Inventory, and I was like, a customer is not going to understand that. A customer wants to know, am I going to sleep better? Am I going to wake up feeling more refreshed? But it's our job as scientists and in the industry to help communicate these clinical benefits into something a consumer is going to understand, because consumers don't understand Eck depressive indexes, Pittsburgh, sleep relaxes, etc. What they do understand is how they're going to feel, and are they going to feel better taking that product? Alex Glover discusses the necessity of translating complex scientific mechanisms into tangible consumer outcomes to drive product sales and customer retention.

## Consumer Insights
**Translating Science**
**Alex** emphasizes that while researchers focus on biological mechanisms like sirtuins, telomeres, or **NAD**, consumers prioritize functional benefits. Customers do not use clinical language; they want to know if a product will help them play with grandchildren, walk without pain, or sleep more refreshingly. **Alex** notes that the highest sales in the **Holland & Barrett** own-label portfolio come from products with clearly communicated benefits for joint function, brain function, and comfort.

**Market Realities**
**Alex** highlights a significant gap in consumer understanding regarding longevity science. In a survey of over 1,000 people, not a single respondent knew what **NAD** was. While there is high interest in "cellular health," consumer definitions are vague, covering everything from fertility to immunity. This suggests that marketing novel ingredients requires bridging the gap between clinical biomarkers and everyday feelings.

## Product Strategy
**Evidence Based Interventions**
**Alex** argues that cost-effective, traditional nutritional interventions often have stronger evidence bases than newer technologies. Examples include:
* **Fiber**: Reduces coronary heart disease risk by approximately 9% per seven grams of intake.
* **Vitamin D**: Highly cost-effective, costing roughly two cents per 10 microgram serving.
* **Curcumin**: A top-selling ingredient globally (one bottle sold per minute) that supports joint flexibility and reduces systemic inflammation.

**The Longevity Gap**
The discussion contrasts the "longevity" category—which implies living longer—with the goal of helping people "live better." **Alex** points out that many industry players get stuck in the "blue sections" of research, focusing on mechanisms and biomarkers rather than clinical outcomes. The primary questions from retailers and customers remain: "When am I going to feel a benefit?" and "How much is it going to cost?"

**Two Waves** is a digital platform designed to streamline the manufacturing ecosystem between brands, manufacturers, and ingredient suppliers.

## Market Challenges
The manufacturing market is projected by **Grandview Research** to grow at over 12 percent annually, exceeding $60 billion by 2030. However, current processes suffer from significant inefficiencies:
* Lack of visibility in specific product categories.
* Incomplete inquiries and fragmented communication across multiple email threads.
* High operational costs due to wasted time organizing data and searching for agreements.
* Lost opportunities resulting from missed offers or inquiries that do not reach the right partners.

## Platform Solutions
**Viktor** and **Matthew** introduced **Two Waves** as a tool to centralize quoting and negotiation through several key modules:
* **New Partnerships**: Instead of one-to-one outreach, one inquiry automatically reaches all verified manufacturers within a specific category, allowing for rapid comparison of structured offers.
* **Standardized Quoting**: The platform uses structured templates tailored to product categories to eliminate "communication noise" and ensure all key information is present.
* **Negotiation Management**: Users can manage quoting variants and track the full history of negotiations in a single location. 
* **Feedback Loops**: If an inquiry or offer is declined, the system provides a specific reason to improve future interactions.

## Security Infrastructure
**Matthew** addressed the risks associated with traditional communication methods like phone calls and emails, where data control is easily lost once information enters an inbox. To mitigate these risks, **Two Waves** implements:
* Mandatory company verification for all users to ensure participants are interacting only with verified entities.
* Enhanced control over how sensitive information is shared during the initial stages of business relationships.

summary.Summary:
The day's closing panel brought together a retailer (Alex Glover, Holland & Barrett), a CDMO (Martina), an ingredient developer (Matt), a food lawyer (Joanna) and a pharmaceutical company (Alexandra). The moderator asked what each wants in the next two or three years, then turned to regulation, supply and AI.

They agreed that the consumer comes first. Alexandra wanted evidence-based claims and better communication, Martina a focus on what consumers actually need, and Alex a few claims done well, starting from the consumer's problem rather than piling on ingredients. Matt wanted a revolution in clinical trials: high-dose studies in people with real problems, published where consumers' chatbots will find them.

On regulation they differed in tone. Joanna wants food law to be a shield for innovators, though the claims system was written for vitamins. Matt was blunter: a three-year longer approval in Europe than in the US almost makes innovation impossible.

On supply, Matt warned of a fish oil shortage reaching shelves next summer. Alex described pre-bought stock and protecting the claim shoppers buy. Joanna said blaming the supplier is no defence.

On AI they wanted a human in the loop and peer-reviewed sources, and Matt warned that anyone who cannot use AI will not be able to work in two years.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Matt: trials in this industry study healthy people for short periods, so effects look small; he would run high-dose studies in people with real problems and publish, because consumers will find it through chatbots [02:52].
- Alex: consumers want evidence but not the EFSA wording; "throwing the kitchen sink" (90 plus ingredients, 35 claims) muddles the message; do a few things well for a defined audience [08:33].
- Joanna: EU food law and the claims regulation were written for vitamin C and D; innovators must combine what is legally possible with showing what trials found; food law should be "a shield", not "a heartbreak" [05:36].
- Matt: same safety package, three years longer approval in Europe than the US; cost today, income later, so the delay "almost makes the innovation impossible" [14:53].
- Matt: fish oil supply is collapsing for aquaculture now and reaches supplement shelves next summer; aquaculture buys the alternatives with higher willingness to pay [18:48].
- Alex: H&B holds up to nine months of pre-purchased stock on core lines; shoppers give three or four seconds at shelf, so protect the claim they buy (heart, eye) and find the alternative [19:36].

The panel discussed the evolving landscape of the nutraceutical industry, focusing on scientific evidence, regulatory challenges, and technological integration.

## Industry Trends
**Alexandra**, **Matt**, and **Alex** highlighted the increasing demand for evidence-based products and high-quality communication.
*   **Alexandra** emphasized that consumers are increasingly well-informed but often rely on unqualified sources, necessitating better communication of factual ingredient claims.
*   **Matt** suggested a revolution in clinical trials, advocating for high-dose studies on individuals with actual health problems rather than healthy subjects to generate more meaningful data.
*   **Alex** noted that consumers prioritize solving specific problems and prefer clear, specialized messaging over brands that attempt to market too many ingredients or claims simultaneously.

## Regulatory Challenges
**Joanna** and **Martina** addressed the friction between innovation and legal frameworks.
*   **Joanna** explained that current food laws were designed for common ingredients like vitamin C and D, making it difficult for innovators to use clinical trial data to support new claims. She urged R&D teams to involve lawyers early in the development process to ensure compliance is a "shield" rather than a "heartbreak."
*   **Martina** observed that legislation often acts as an obstacle for CDMOs and advised businesses not to simply chase every market gap but to focus on deep understanding and consumer needs.
*   **Matt** raised concerns regarding the speed of European regulations compared to the **U.S.**, noting that a three-year delay in approval can make the net present value of new ingredients economically unviable.

## Supply and Technology
The discussion concluded with the impact of supply chain volatility and artificial intelligence.
*   **Matt** warned of a looming collapse in the fish oil supply chain due to aquaculture industry competition and potential traceability issues involving illegal fishing. 
*   **Alex** noted that retailers must proactively manage lead times and prepare for price increases or shifts in consumer preference if core ingredients like omega-3 become unavailable.
*   **Joanna** and **Alexandra** discussed the role of **AI**, noting its utility in searching peer-reviewed databases and managing factory sensors. **Joanna** stressed the importance of keeping a "human in the loop" to maintain legal integrity and trust, while **Matt** predicted that proficiency in operating **AI** tools will become a mandatory job requirement within two years.

Source: Otter.ai recording "Marit - HMT - Remedy CMO", https://otter.ai/u/bK_DMxHJzVgH8AgUv_VzIp24x3Y, recorded 23 Oct 2026 10:03, 11m 31s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:24] Speaker 2: Thank you. Hello, good morning, everyone. I'm actually really happy to see that the room is quite full because after last night I was expecting less people to be here. To be honest, and thank you for the introduction. So my name is Marit Weinstra, and yes, I'm from H and D. So you said it very well. We do branding and innovation for food and supplements. And today I'm talking about beyond probiotics because when Paolo asked me, "Can you talk about probiotics?" First I thought, "Okay, in 10 minutes, what's there's only so much you can say in 10 minutes about probiotics." But I thought let's make it a little bit easier for myself, and let's talk about beyond the probiotics. Because in the end, if you work in probiotics, you also need to understand what's happening beyond probiotics. We have prebiotics, we have fibers, we have postbiotics. So the market is becoming much bigger. So it's important to understand what is happening. Yes. Okay. So I don't think I have to tell you that probiotics in general have increased in popularity in the past years. So both the sales have increased. Have increased. The consumption has has increased, and more and more people are aware of the effects of any type of biotic, basically, and the gut health. So this is of course really good for our industry. But when we look at the at the market, we see more and more products being launched every day in different formats, new ingredients, new health benefits, so it's becoming really a jungle of products. And imagine yourself as a consumer standing in front of the shelves or looking online for what products you want to buy. How can you understand which product you need to choose? Because there is so much available. And in the end, and I think Alex told that very well yesterday. In the end, the consumer just wants to understand which product is actually right for me, and this is where we can still do a lot of work in this industry because there are too many options out there, but there's not enough clarity in this industry. And consumers even say that they don't feel that informed about probiotics, maybe they know that it's good for them. They know they need to do something about their gut health, but do they really understand what it is and what it does? Well, we still have a lot to achieve here. So to talk about and to understand where we are today and what you need to be aware of to really win in this market today, I want to go a little bit back in time and also give you an understanding of how did we actually get here and what what happened in this in this whole category and how has the market evolved. So it actually started with Yakult and the understanding that there can be good and bad bacteria because initially it was okay, bacteria are bad for you, but then there came the understanding and especially the education that there can also be good bacteria. And actually, how the category was born was right away from a really good point of view because it was right away born as a daily ritual. And we all know that if you want the biotics to be successful in your body, you kind of need to take it on a daily basis. So the category was born as a daily ritual in a very convenient format, and yeah, something that you can easily take every day.
[03:52] Speaker 3: 10 o'clock already should be now.
[03:53] Speaker 2: But then the challenge was: okay, you have this benefit
[03:56] Speaker 4: of it supports your gut flora, which is very
[03:59] Speaker 2: intangible because of the bacteria, and this. where Danone Activia actually led that second wave, and they try to make the invisible benefits more tangible by talking about the digestion. And you see that in their old logo, the way that they branded their strains, and they really help to yeah educate more around the benefits that probiotics can have in your gut, but this also led to the competition of more bacteria is better, and where where brands started competing on the CFU count. And the third era, this is where we also started to understand. Okay, but if it doesn't arrive alive in your gut, then actually it doesn't really work. So this is where the technology became the story, and survival became the promise, so that it has to survive, arrive alive in your gut. But as you can imagine, we are moving now further away from the consumer and helping them understand, okay, but what does it actually do for you? And where we are now is where we shifted from adding to nourishing, and this is where the market now starts to educate on, okay, you already your gut is an ecosystem, and we need to nourish that, we need to strengthen that, and this is opening a whole new world because this is where we start creating new language in the category. So we move from strains and bacteria. We can actually talk about the ecosystem, the gut barrier. This is where fermentation becomes an important term, even a whole food approach. So the question is really changing from what is in the product to what does it actually do for me. And the gut also became the gateway because when we move the focus from just bacteria to actually the gut barrier and the whole ecosystem, the gut barrier is also where it meets the rest of your body. So this is where the story becomes much bigger, and this is also why the why the category really exploded because it's not only about digestion anymore. So this also means that now that the the market has become so much bigger, and we're not only talking about bacteria anymore, that there are also new rules that define actually what win in the category today. So I'm gonna show you the four different rules. I don't think you can see it very well, but the next slide you should see them. So the first rule is from more is better to quality and proven. And as I said before, you still have a lot of shelves where you see 50 billion, 80 billion, 100 billions of bacteria, and to be honest, it doesn't really mean anything to the consumer. They don't understand what is that difference, and they probably feel that more is better. But what we're seeing that numbers alone don't build trust anymore with the consumer, and how you can build trust with the consumer is also not to focus anymore on the generic gut benefits, but really try to be an expert in your own niche. And this is where this brand from the U.S. does a good job. So they they are based on the Acromancia strain, and they really focus on metabolic health and weight management. Then the second rule is from simply adding bacteria to feeding your whole ecosystem. And as I said before, this is really opening a new world and language that the consumer actually understands much better, because this is where we can talk about nourishing, nourishing what you already have, the diversity of plants that you need to actually feed the bacteria that are in your gut. So the language becomes more relatable for the consumer. You can actually see it because bacteria you don't see it, but when you start talking about fibers and plants, it becomes much more tangible. And this is also where you can be more in control as a consumer because you can actually proactively do something about it. You can proactively feed your gut yourself. So this is where you see now mainly the fiber brands that are talking about this, but also where it's not about having just one fiber, one prebiotic fiber anymore, but really have that diversity, and then we have the third rule, and that is from belief and promise to measurable and felt benefits. And for years, the benefit was quite invisible. It was about supporting a healthy gut flora, and that is relevant for those who actually understand a bit more about gut health and the importance of probiotics, for instance. But what we're seeing now is that early adopters they actually start measuring the benefits. So they do microbiome tests. They use different apps to actually measure the effect that it has on their on their body. And this is where we see the mass market consumers, so let's say most consumers that are out there, they want to feel the benefits. So for them, if they use it and they don't feel the benefits, they won't continue to use your products. So these are the consumers that will only continue to buy once they feel difference. And you don't see the example very well, but this is where you see brands that start communicating and creating the right expectations for consumers. So, what can you actually feel when you use this product for one week, for one month? And I know this is maybe not so science-based, but this is actually easier for consumers to understand, and this is what they will measure their expectations against, and then the last rule, and that is from functional supplements to everyday food and formats. And I don't want to say that supplements are not relevant anymore, but in the end, consumers will stick with what they like and what they find desirable. So this is where Poppy is a good example, not because it's a good quality product necessarily, but because they really turned it into a format that people like. So before the probiotics were really designed around the product, but now it needs to be designed really around the consumer, and the value is really moving from what is inside the product to what the consumer gets, and I already hear you thinking, "Oh, but you're only showing American examples. We cannot use those claims here in Europe," and that is actually where branding comes in. So in Europe, you can't claim most of it, and that's when the brand has to carry it. And that has also been Activia's strategy for a long time, so it's branding your stream. Yeah, branding of course in the name, in the page, and that is what we call building your double IP. Marit Weinstra of HMT, a branding and innovation agency for food and supplements, opened the probiotic programme. Her question was how to win in a biotics market that has grown into a jungle of products, where consumers say they do not feel informed.

She traced four eras. Yakult made good bacteria a daily ritual. Danone Activia made digestion benefits tangible, which led brands to compete on CFU count. Marit Weinstra from **HMT** discusses the evolution of the probiotic market and shifting consumer expectations toward holistic gut health.

## Market Evolution
The probiotic category has moved through several distinct eras, transitioning from basic awareness to complex ecosystem management.
*   **First Era**: Focused on the concept of "good" vs "bad" bacteria, popularized by **Yakult** as a daily ritual.
*   **Second Era**: Led by **Danone Activia**, which focused on making intangible benefits like digestion more tangible via branding.
*   **Third Era**: Centered on technology and survival, where the primary promise was ensuring bacteria arrive alive in the gut.
*   **Current Era**: Shifting from simply adding bacteria to nourishing the entire gut ecosystem, focusing on terms like the gut barrier and fermentation.

## Strategic Shifts
To succeed in the current "jungle" of products, brands must follow four new industry rules to build consumer trust and clarity.
*   **Quality over Quantity**: Moving away from competing solely on high CFU counts (e.g., 50 billion or 100 billion) toward proven, niche expertise such as metabolic health.
*   **Ecosystem Nourishment**: Transitioning from adding single strains to providing plant diversity and fibers that proactively feed existing gut flora.
*   **Measurable Benefits**: Shifting from invisible promises to felt or measured results, utilizing microbiome tests or apps for early adopters while ensuring mass-market consumers feel immediate physical differences.
*   **Consumer-Centric Formats**: Moving from functional supplements toward desirable everyday food formats, similar to how **Poppi** approaches the category.

## Branding Strategy
Because many health claims are restricted in Europe compared to the U.S., brands must rely on emotional value rather than just rational science. 
*   Building a "double IP" involves combining rational scientific evidence with an emotional brand identity to ensure long-term protection and market presence. 
*   Success requires turning scientific innovation into a consumer-centric value proposition that provides clarity amidst excessive market options.

[00:42] Speaker 2: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for being here today. And thank you, Pavel, for the opportunity. My name is Ariel Annoni, and I'm responsible for human health business across Central East Europe, Middle Eastern Africa in Novonasis. Today, I would like to share a simple story. It's a story about science can become a successful consumer product. It's also a story about a partnership. Because in probiotic, success is not only about having a good ingredient. It's about having the right science, the right quality, and the right manufacturing partner, and the right brand strategy, and this is exactly why we are here today. Before taking talking biotic, let me introduce Novonasis. Novonasis was created by the combination of Novozyme and Christian Hansen, with two huge companies with a long history in bioscience. Together, we bring more than 100 years of expertise in microorganism and biotechnology. This experience gives our customer the confidence that they are working with a strong and stable partner. For us, innovation is important, but also reliability, because consumers and customer need both. *   **Quality Standards**: They offer both GMP pharma-standard facilities for high-end APIs and conventional GMP food-grade sites, supported by validation experts.
*   **Services**: Capabilities include providing probiotics, postbiotics, customized mixtures, and a "made-for-you" service for third-party strain development.

## Product Portfolio
The presentation highlights two primary areas of investment: women's health and healthy aging.

**Women's Health: CA15**
**CA15** is a patented strain isolated from vaginal samples in 2022. 
*   **Efficacy**: Clinical studies involving 200 women showed significant reduction in symptoms of bacterial vaginosis and vaginal candidiasis, such as burning, itching, and inflammation.
*   **Diagnostic Results**: Post-treatment (10 days) and one month after washout, 98% of subjects showed restored pH ranges and 92% had negative amine tests.
*   **Mechanism**: The strain survives gastrointestinal transit, colonizes the vagina, promotes natural lactobacilli like *G. acidophilus*, and reduces pathogens like *Gardnerella vaginalis*.

**Healthy Aging: Symbio**
**Symbio** is a synergistic mixture of *L. paracasi* and *L. rhamnosus* isolated from the Italian Marche region.
*   **Clinical Findings**: In a double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 97 subjects over six months, **Symbio** increased gut microbiota diversity (Akkermansia, Bifidobacteria) and short-chain fatty acids like butyrate.
*   **Inflammation & Muscle Mass**: Results showed a 43% reduction in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and improved insulin growth factor one levels to combat sarcopenia.
*   **Longevity**: Blood analysis indicated a decrease in the rate of telomere shortening, a key marker of biological aging.

summary.Summary:
Two suppliers shared this slot. Miguel of SPI Pharma, joined mid-talk by the recording, argued that CDMOs can grow by moving probiotics and other actives into new dosage forms, and showed three concepts.

The first was a chewable probiotic tablet, made on a low-moisture platform and pressed gently so the bacteria survive. The second was effervescent hydration formats, kept stable with a modified sodium bicarbonate; a light fizz also helps mask bitterness. The third was fast-melt tablets for children, older people who struggle to swallow, and anyone who dislikes pills. His close, aimed at the capsule maker ACG: do not ask consumers to swallow another capsule.

Mihail Jakubowski of Nordic Biotic then presented a supplier of clinically tested probiotic strains, sold with exclusivity by territory. Its work runs from genomics and metabolomics to human studies. He showed a stress and sleep blend tested on 227 students at exam time, saying the results, received the week before, proved efficacy on sleep quality and stress. He also showed a blend aimed at microplastics, with its human study still in progress.

His close was an invitation to develop new products together.

The meeting focused on innovative probiotic dosage forms and clinically tested probiotic strain technologies.

## Dosage Form Innovation
**Miguel** from **SPI Pharma** presented advanced delivery systems designed to improve consumer experience and stability.
*   **Composol Pro Tab**: A polyol-based, low water activity platform used to create chewable probiotic tablets with low compression forces to ensure probiotic survival.
*   **Effer Soda**: A partially transformed sodium bicarbonate product that creates a protective layer, enhancing stability in effervescent tablets, stick packs, or sachets. This technology can also produce a "delicate fizz" in fast-melting solutions to mask bitterness.
*   **Orally Disintegrating Tablets (ODT)**: Fast-melting platforms designed for populations with dysphagia, such as children and the elderly, allowing for consumption without water.

## Probiotic Research
**Mihail Jakubowski** of **Nordic Biotic** detailed scientific advancements in specialized probiotic strains and their metabolic functions.
*   **Northbiotic Mental Balance**: Developed with the **Polish Academy of Sciences**, this blend uses **Lactobacillus plantarum 140** (producing GABA) and **Bifidobacterium breve 010** (producing vitamin B free). An eight-week study of 227 students demonstrated statistical efficacy in improving sleep quality and managing stress.
*   **Microplastic Management**: A novel approach using two specific strains for gut cleansing:
    1.  **Lactobacillus acidophilus 120**: Aggregates and binds microplastic particles.
    2.  **Lactobacillus fermentum 160**: Pushes microplastics away from the mucosal lining to facilitate removal.
*   Human studies regarding the microplastic-binding technology are currently in progress.

## Strategic Partnerships
Both speakers emphasized opportunities for collaborative development between manufacturers and researchers. 
*   **Miguel** invited participants to use **SPI Pharma's** concept-driven approach to expand existing portfolios into new dosage forms like hydration sticks or chewable probiotics. 
*   **Mihail Jakubowski** proposed the **Plastic Gut-Free Initiative**, inviting brand owners and CDMOs to participate in co-development projects centered on microbiome research and genomics.
